UNIT.subject: Biology
UNIT.strand: Strand 2.0: Anatomy and Physiology of Plants
UNIT.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
UNIT.content:
• Meaning and significance of growth and development
• Structure of the seed (monocots and dicots)
• Seed dormancy (meaning, significance, causes and ways of breaking seed dormancy)
• Germination (process, types and conditions necessary for germination)
• Primary and secondary growth
• Measurement of growth and growth curves
• Role of hormones in plant growth and development (include apical dominance)
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) distinguish between growth and development in living organisms,
b) relate structures of monocot and dicot seeds to their functions,
c) outline causes and ways of breaking dormancy in seeds,
d) investigate conditions necessary for seed germination,
e) investigate types of germination in plants,
f) illustrate primary and secondary growth in flowering plants,
g) demonstrate the role of hormones in plant growth and development,
h) appreciate the importance of growth and development in plants.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Citizenship: The learner solves problems in the community by sharing the seedlings from the established tree nursery.
• Learning to Learn: The learner reflects on their own work and adjusts accordingly while carrying out activities to demonstrate ways of breaking seed dormancy.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners investigate the farmer's problem of uneven germination and growth of maize and beans.
• Communication and Collaboration: Learners share evidence and findings in group investigations.
• Creativity and Imagination: Learners design experiments and build and revise models of germination and growth.
• Digital Literacy: Learners use the maize and bean time-lapse videos and other digital resources, with teacher-prepared alternatives when offline.
UNIT.values:
• Unity: The learner works harmoniously with others while carrying out experiments to investigate conditions necessary for seed germination.
• Patriotism: The learner demonstrates devotion to the country/community while sharing seedlings with the school community for environmental conservation, and links healthy plant growth to Kenya's food security.
• Responsibility: Learners care for the experimental seeds and follow procedures.
• Integrity: Learners record actual observations rather than changing results to match predictions.
• Respect: Learners listen to and consider other learners' explanations.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: Learners post questions about the maize and bean phenomenon on the Driving Question Board.
• Developing and Using Models: Learners draw an initial model in Lesson 1 and revise it as they learn about seeds, dormancy, germination, growth and hormones.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: Learners test conditions for germination, compare hypogeal and epigeal germination, and break dormancy using maize and bean seeds.
• Analyzing and Interpreting Data: Learners record seedling height and stem width and draw growth curves.
• Constructing Explanations: Learners explain the differences in germination, emergence and growth using evidence.
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: Learners defend explanations and respond to peers' ideas.
• Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information: Learners use readings, videos and microscope sections to share findings.
UNIT.pcis:
• Financial Literacy: The learner explores ways of generating income while selling seedlings to members of the community.
• Prevention of Global Warming: The learner mitigates the effects of global warming by establishing a tree nursery and distributing seedlings in the community.
• Food security and nutrition, sustainable agriculture and agricultural productivity: Understanding germination and growth helps improve crop establishment and yields of maize and beans.
• Climate change and adaptation, environmental and water conservation: Learners relate rainfall and soil moisture to germination and growth.
• Technology and innovation: Learners use time-lapse videos and plant hormone applications in agriculture.
UNIT.careers:
• Agronomist: How can farmers improve crop establishment and growth?
• Seed Technologist: Why do some seeds germinate while others fail to germinate?
• Agricultural Research Scientist: What conditions produce better germination and plant growth?
• Plant Physiologist: What processes and hormones control plant growth?
• Plant Breeder: Can varieties be developed that germinate and grow better under Kenyan conditions?
• Agricultural Extension Officer: How can this knowledge be transferred to farmers?
UNIT.focus: This unit uses a farmer's maize and bean field after rainfall as an anchoring phenomenon to explain why seeds germinate at different times, some fail to germinate, and plants grow differently. Learners investigate seed structure, dormancy, germination, primary and secondary growth, growth measurement and hormones using locally available seeds and low-cost materials. They revise a cumulative model and use the Driving Question Board throughout, and the unit ends with a tree nursery project using natural rooting hormones.
UNIT.phenomenon: A farmer plants maize and beans on the same day after rainfall. Time-lapse videos show the seeds germinating and the seedlings growing. Some seeds germinate within a few days, while others take longer, and some fail to germinate even though they appear healthy. As the plants grow, stems become taller and thicker, roots extend deeper, and some plants develop branches. It is puzzling because the seeds were planted together under the same rain, yet they behave differently. Learners must explain what causes these differences in germination, emergence and growth.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Maize seedlings (monocot) emerge with the seed remaining underground, while bean seedlings (dicot) push up with seed leaves above the soil.
• Healthy-looking seeds fail to germinate until the seed coat is scratched or soaked in water, as with some hard-coated seeds.
• A tree trunk becomes thicker each year while the seedling tip keeps growing taller, shown by annual rings and elongating shoots.
• Pinching off the tip of a plant such as a bean or tea shoot makes side branches grow, while a stem cutting treated with bulb onion or Aloe extract grows roots.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How does growth occur in plants?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: The learner gets to know the phenomena. Watch the time-lapse videos of maize and beans (Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section; Growing corn time lapse), draw initial models, write questions and post them on the Driving Question Board. Question raised: What is growth and development?
Lesson 2: Meaning of growth and development. Structure of the seed (monocot and dicot). Discuss the meaning of growth and development, then observe, draw and label monocot and dicot seeds and discuss the functions of the structures with peers. Question raised: What is seed dormancy?
Lesson 3: Seed dormancy. Examine seed specimens to identify causes of seed dormancy and discuss with peers; carry out activities to demonstrate ways of breaking seed dormancy (Khan Academy video on seed dormancy where available). Question raised: How does germination occur?
Lesson 4: Germination (process, types and conditions necessary for germination). Use maize and bean seeds to investigate conditions necessary for germination and carry out experiments to investigate types of germination. Question raised: How do plants show growth?
Lesson 5: Germination continued. Set up and analyze the germination investigations, compare hypogeal and epigeal germination, and revise models. Question raised: How do plants show growth?
Lesson 6: Primary and secondary growth. Observe sections of stems under a microscope or photomicrographs, draw and label them, and use drawings and models to illustrate stages of secondary growth. Question raised: How can you measure growth in plants?
Lesson 7: Primary and secondary growth continued. Model secondary growth in a woody dicot, and use seedlings to determine regions of growth in plants and discuss with peers. Question raised: How can you measure growth in plants?
Lesson 8: Measurement of growth and growth curves. Record seedling height and stem width data, draw growth curves and discuss with peers. Question raised: Do we have hormones in plants?
Lesson 9: Role of hormones in plant growth and development. Watch a video showing the effects of plant hormones, read on the functions of major plant hormones including apical dominance, and relate them to agriculture.
Lesson 10: Synthesis and application. Complete the final cumulative model, revisit the Driving Question Board, explain the farmer's maize and bean differences, and plan the tree nursery project using stem cuttings and natural rooting hormones such as bulb onion, Aloe and cinnamon.

LESSONS.title: The Farmer's Puzzle: Why Do Maize and Beans Behave Differently After the Same Rain?
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: germination, emergence, growth, development, maize, beans, seed, root, shoot, time-lapse, initial model, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon: maize and beans planted on the same day after rainfall germinate, emerge and grow differently. Learners watch the time-lapse videos, draw initial models, write baseline explanations and generate questions that open the Driving Question Board (DQB).
slo.knowledge: Learners begin to recognise that seeds planted together under the same rain can differ in germination time, emergence and growth pattern (stem height and thickness, root depth, branching). They name what they notice and wonder about, and identify the question to pursue next: What is growth and development? This links to the sub-strand outcome: distinguish between growth and development in living organisms.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (drawing and labelling initial models of a maize seed and a bean seed); Asking questions; Observing and recording patterns from time-lapse video; Constructing explanations (initial, unmarked); Communicating ideas in simple, clear scientific English.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity and willingness to wonder; respect for others' ideas (Unity: the learner works harmoniously with others); honesty in sharing baseline thinking without fear of being wrong; appreciation of the importance of growth and development in plants. Learning to Learn: the learner reflects on their own ideas and expects to adjust them later.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 introduces the phenomenon and creates the need to know. Learners' baseline models and questions go onto the DQB and drive every later lesson: seed structure, dormancy, conditions for germination, types of germination, primary and secondary growth, growth curves and hormones. Learners return to these Day 1 models at the end of the unit to revise them with evidence. The lesson ends with the new question: What is growth and development?
slo.safetyNotes: If learners handle real seeds, they should wash hands afterwards and must not eat seeds that are treated (dressed) with pesticide, often pink or red. Keep seeds away from the mouth. Arrange seating so learners can see the screen or demonstration without crowding. Keep walkways clear during DQB posting.

LESSONS.overview: Teacher opens with a short story about a farmer in Nakuru County (Rift Valley) who plants maize and beans on the same day after the long rains and is puzzled by the results. Learners predict what will happen, then watch two time-lapse videos (Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section; Growing corn time lapse #greentimelapse #gtl #timelapse). If there is no electricity or internet, the teacher uses a prepared alternative: a sequence of 6 to 8 large chalk or chart drawings or photographs showing day 0, 3, 7, 14 and 25, plus a teacher-narrated script, and real soaked and sprouted maize and bean seeds on a tray. Learners record 'I notice' and 'I wonder' statements using Think-Pair-Share, then individually draw initial models of a maize seed and a bean seed, showing what happens after planting, the root and shoot emerging, and development over time, with arrows and labels. They complete the sentence starters, which are not marked right or wrong. In small groups they write questions on sticky notes or cards and post them on the DQB, sorting them into categories. The class agrees on the first new question, 'What is growth and development?', which leads into Lesson 2. Learners keep their drawings in a folder for revision at the end of the unit.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners listen to the farmer's story: 'Mama Wanjiru in Molo plants maize and beans on the same morning after the first heavy rains. The seeds look healthy. After one week, some seeds have sprouted, some are late, and a few have not come up at all.' Learners individually write a quick prediction in their notebooks: 'I think the maize and the beans will ______ because ______.' They also complete 'I think a seed needs ________ in order to germinate because…'. Then they Think-Pair-Share with a partner, comparing which seeds they think will come up first and why. They share predictions with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the story slowly with a local accent and actions, then say: 'Mama Wanjiru planted maize and beans on the same day, in the same rain. What do you think will happen to the seeds? Take 10 to 15 seconds of silent thinking time. Write one prediction.' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds, silently scanning the room. Then say: 'Turn to your partner and share. You have 2 minutes.' Walk around and listen without correcting. Cold-call 4 learners (2 who predict maize first, 2 who predict beans first) with: 'Tell us what you predicted and why.' Ask a follow-up to 2 of them: 'What makes you say that?' Record all predictions on the board under the headings 'Maize first', 'Beans first', 'Same time', 'Not sure'. Do not say which is correct. Say: 'Let us keep these predictions and test them against what we see.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share (Predict-Observe-Explain, predict step): individual thinking first ensures every learner commits to an idea before seeing evidence. Pair talk lets learners rehearse and refine their language, and whole-class sharing reveals the range of ideas (including misconceptions) that the class will test against the videos.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: tick which learners write a prediction (not blank) and give a reason using 'because'. Listen for preconceptions such as 'big seeds always grow first', 'seeds need only water', 'seeds that look healthy must germinate', or 'plants grow only from the top'. Note 3 to 4 learners whose ideas to revisit. Indicator: at least 80% of learners have a written prediction with a reason before the video starts.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners watch the two time-lapse videos: 'Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section' and 'Growing corn time lapse #greentimelapse #gtl #timelapse'. They watch twice: first with no writing, just watching; second while jotting notes in a two-column table 'I notice' and 'I wonder'. They pay attention to: which seed splits or emerges first, the root growing down before or after the shoot grows up, how the stem becomes taller and thicker, how roots extend deeper (soil cross-section), branching or leaves appearing, and the seeds that do not sprout. If there is no connectivity, learners observe the teacher's alternative: day-by-day pictures and a tray of real soaked maize and bean seeds (day 0), partly sprouted seeds (day 3 to 5) and seedlings (day 10 or more), passed around by group or viewed at the front. They compare the maize and bean sequences, sharing observations with their group.
framework.teacherMoves: Before playing: 'Watch carefully. The first time, just watch. The second time, write what you notice and what you wonder.' Play the bean video, pause at 3 points (for example when the root first appears, when the shoot emerges above the soil, when leaves open) and ask: 'What do you see happening right now?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners each time (6 learners total). Repeat for the maize video. Ask: 'What is the same in both plants? What is different?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, cold-call 3 learners. Prompt precision: 'Which part came out first, the root or the shoot? How do you know?' If there is no power: hold up each picture, give 10 to 15 seconds for learners to look, narrate neutral facts only ('This is day 5'), and let learners name what they see. Pass the real seeds around in groups of 5 to 6 with the instruction 'Look, do not open yet'. Use simple English and write new words on the board with meanings: germination, emergence, shoot, root, stem.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (observe step): watching the same phenomenon twice moves learners from general impressions to specific, recordable patterns. The 'I notice / I wonder' table separates evidence from questions, so that the later explanations and DQB questions are rooted in observations rather than guesses.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect 'I notice' and 'I wonder' tables from 5 learners at random. Look for observable indicators: at least 3 specific observations (e.g. 'the root came out before the shoot', 'the maize leaf was rolled', 'the bean stem was bent like a hook') and at least 2 wonderings. Oral probing: 'What did you see that surprised you?' Note the learners who only write general statements such as 'the plant grew' and prompt them to add details like the order and the part.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work individually first, drawing and labelling their initial model. On an A4 page or notebook spread, they (1) draw a maize seed and a bean seed, (2) show what they think happens after planting, (3) show the root and shoot emerging, (4) show how the plant develops over time (for example Day 0, Day 5, Day 14, Day 25), and (5) add arrows and labels to explain their ideas, including what the seed gets from the soil and rain. They then complete the sentence starters: 'I think maize and bean plants grow differently because…', 'I notice that…', 'I wonder why…', and 'I think a seed needs ________ in order to germinate because…'. In their groups they use Think-Pair-Share to explain their model to a partner, and then each pair shares one idea with their group of 4 to 6. Learners add a different colour pen to mark ideas they borrow or change after discussion, so that their original thinking stays visible.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are scientists like Prof. Wangari Maathai, who observed trees, asked why, and tried to explain. Today you will show your first thinking. There is no right or wrong answer. I am not marking this.' Show a quick example on the board of how to label (arrow to root, label 'root'), using a non-maize, non-bean example such as a sukuma wiki seed, so you do not give the answer. Give 10 minutes for individual drawing. WAIT TIME: 10 to 15 seconds after each question you ask during the task. Circulate and ask 5 to 6 learners: 'Tell me about this arrow. What is happening here?' and 'Why did you draw the root there?' Do not correct; write down interesting ideas and misconceptions. Then say: 'Turn to your partner and explain your model in 1 minute each.' Cold-call 3 learners to share one idea from their partner's model (not their own) to build listening: 'What did your partner show that you had not thought about?' Finish with: 'Keep your first model safe. At the end of this unit you will come back and see how your thinking has changed.' Collect or store the models in folders marked with learner names. If many learners are in class, rotate through the groups using the checklist rather than every individual.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model-based reasoning and Think-Pair-Share: drawing forces learners to make their thinking visible (what is inside the seed, what is needed, what changes over time). Explaining to a partner exposes gaps in the models. The unmarked baseline becomes the starting point for later model revision, so learners see learning as changing their own ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist for models: tick if the learner (a) draws both seeds, (b) shows the root and shoot emerging, (c) shows change over time, (d) uses at least 3 labels and arrows, and (e) gives a reason in the 'because' sentences. Record misconceptions such as 'the seed grows from the top only', 'the seed is dead until it is wet', 'the plant gets all its food from the soil', 'maize and beans grow the same way'. These are not marked. Indicator: at least 80% of the models have labelled arrows and a written reason, forming a baseline for the end-of-unit comparison.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 to 6 discuss: 'What questions do you have after watching the videos and considering the farmer's problem?' Each learner writes at least one question on a sticky note or a cut piece of paper (cards from old exercise books or manila paper work well), and the group chooses 2 to 3 of their best questions. Groups post their questions on the DQB (a chart or a wall section headed 'Why do maize and beans germinate, emerge and grow differently?'). Then, as a class, they sort the questions into clusters, for example: 'Inside the seed', 'Water, air, warmth', 'Seeds that did not germinate', 'How plants get taller and thicker', 'Roots and shoots', 'Why maize and beans differ'. They identify a question that appears many times, 'What is growth and development?', as the first to investigate in Lesson 2.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the driving question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' Say: 'Now it is your turn to be the questioners. In your group, what questions do you have? Write one question per note. Start with Why, How, What or When.' Model one good question: 'Why did some seeds that looked healthy not germinate?' and one weak question and improve it: 'Is maize good?' becomes 'How does maize grow differently from beans?' Give 5 minutes for writing. WAIT TIME: 10 to 15 seconds after asking each group to choose their strongest questions. Circulate, and ask 2 groups: 'Can you turn this into a question that we can investigate?' Invite 6 groups (or all groups, if fewer) to read out and post one question each, then ask the class: 'Which questions seem to belong together?' Cold-call 3 learners to suggest the groupings. Point out the repeated question: 'Many of you asked what growth is, and what development is. Are they the same?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, cold-call 2 learners. Then say: 'This is our question for the next lesson: What is growth and development?' Record it clearly on the DQB. Leave space for 'What we have learned' and 'Evidence' columns to be added later. If space is limited, the DQB can be drawn on a sheet of manila paper or the back of a calendar.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the DQB: learners' own questions give them ownership of the unit and a clear purpose for each future lesson. Clustering shows the links between questions (seed structure, conditions, hormones) and helps learners see that one big phenomenon can be broken into smaller investigable parts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the DQB for observable indicators: each group has posted at least 2 questions, with at least one that is investigable (starts with how, why or what causes). Tally how many questions focus on (a) seed structure, (b) conditions for germination, (c) growth and development, (d) differences between maize and beans, to plan upcoming lessons. Oral probing: 'What would we need to do to answer this question?' Note groups that only ask yes/no questions and coach them to rephrase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit their initial model and make a first, small update using a different coloured pen: they add one thing they now notice from the videos that they did not draw before (for example the root emerging before the shoot, the way the maize shoot is covered by a sheath, or the curved bean stem), and one question mark next to a part of the model they are unsure about. They then do a Gallery Walk: groups place their models on desks or walls, and learners move around for about 6 minutes with sticky dots or ticks, leaving a comment such as 'I also thought…' or 'I wonder about…' on at least 2 other models. Finally they complete an exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?' They also record the new question: 'What is growth and development?' The finished models go into a folder as the 'Day 1 model' for revision at the end of the unit.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Models are never finished. Take your coloured pen and add one thing you noticed from the videos. Put a question mark where you are not sure.' Give 5 minutes, WAIT TIME 10 to 15 seconds before taking questions. Set Gallery Walk rules: 'Walk quietly, read kindly, comment on two other models using 'I also thought…' or 'I wonder about…'. We do not say 'wrong' today.' Rotate groups every 2 minutes. After the walk, cold-call 3 learners: 'What idea did you see in another model that was different from yours?' Then summarise: 'Our models show many ideas: some of you think the seed needs water, some warmth, some air or soil. We will test these in the coming lessons.' Distribute exit tickets (half-sheets) and say: 'Write two sentences: What evidence did we gather today? How does this help answer our driving question?' Collect them at the door. Link forward: 'Next time we will begin by asking, what do we mean by growth, and how is it different from development?' Store the models and the DQB safely for the next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision and Gallery Walk: adding evidence from the videos in a different colour shows learners that models change when new evidence appears. Peer review exposes learners to alternative explanations, building the habit of comparing ideas, which will support Claim-Evidence-Reasoning explanations in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket indicators: the learner names at least one specific piece of evidence from the videos (for example 'the root came out first in both seeds') and links it to the driving question in one sentence. Sort the tickets into three piles (clear link, partial link, no link) and note which learners need support with the term 'evidence'. Peer review: check that each learner left at least 2 comments on other models. Model check: look for an added feature in a second colour on at least 80% of the models.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask yourself: (1) Did every learner commit to a prediction and a first model before hearing others' ideas? (2) What were the 3 most common ideas or misconceptions about seeds, germination and growth (for example 'the seed is dead until it gets wet', 'only water is needed', 'plants grow like animals')? (3) Which questions on the DQB can be answered with the investigations planned in this unit, and which need to be reshaped? (4) Was the language manageable for learners, and which words need to be taught more clearly (germination, emergence, development)? (5) If the video was not available, did the pictures and real seeds create enough curiosity? (6) In large classes, were the groups and materials (sticky notes, manila paper, seeds) manageable, and who needs more support next lesson? Keep the baseline models, the exit tickets and a photograph or copy of the DQB for the end-of-unit revision.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In the time-lapse videos and pictures of maize and beans planted together after rain, we observed that the seeds germinated at different times, the root and shoot emerged, stems became taller and thicker, roots went deeper, some plants developed branches, and some seeds did not germinate even though they looked healthy.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the same rain and same planting day do not give the same result for every seed, and that we do not yet know what causes these differences. We drew our first models and learned that ideas can change when we find evidence. We also learned that we need to understand what growth and development mean.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Our first explanation (not yet marked): maize and bean plants may grow differently because of differences in their seeds and in what each seed needs, such as water, air and warmth. We do not yet have evidence, so we have posted our questions on the Driving Question Board. Our next question is: What is growth and development?

LESSONS.title: Meaning of Growth and Development; Structure of Monocot and Dicot Seeds
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: growth, development, monocot, dicot, maize grain, bean seed, testa, pericarp, cotyledon, endosperm, embryo, plumule, radicle, hilum, micropyle, scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza

slo.purpose: Learners distinguish growth from development and relate the structures of maize (monocot) and bean (dicot) seeds to their functions, so they can begin to explain why seeds planted on the same day by a Kenyan farmer germinate, emerge and grow differently.
slo.knowledge: a) Distinguish between growth and development in living organisms. b) Relate structures of monocot and dicot seeds to their functions.
slo.skills: Observing and dissecting seeds; drawing and labelling biological diagrams; comparing and contrasting; communicating in clear scientific English; collaborating in small groups.
slo.attitudes: Unity: works harmoniously with others while examining seeds. Learning to Learn: reflects on own drawings and adjusts them after peer feedback. Appreciation of the importance of growth and development in plants.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 presented the phenomenon: maize and beans planted together after rain behave differently. Lesson 2 establishes what growth and development mean and shows that maize and beans have different internal seed structures (food store in endosperm vs cotyledons). This gives a first possible reason for differences in emergence and early growth, and raises a new question: some seeds that look healthy do not germinate, so what is seed dormancy? That leads into Lesson 3.
slo.safetyNotes: Use blunt scalpels or razor blades only under teacher supervision, or use a thumbnail/knife handled by one group member; cut away from the body on a tile or flat board. Soak seeds for 12-24 hours beforehand to soften them. Do not taste seeds, especially any treated with fungicide/pesticide (often pink or purple coated seed from agrovets). Wash hands after handling. Hand lenses only; never look at the sun.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by recalling the time-lapse of the farmer's maize and beans after rainfall and predicting what is inside a maize grain and a bean seed. Using Think-Pair-Share they define growth (irreversible increase in size/dry mass) and development (changes in form and complexity, differentiation). In groups they then observe pre-soaked maize grains and bean seeds, draw and label them, and discuss the function of each structure with peers. A Gallery Walk lets groups compare drawings. Learners explain, using evidence, how the structure of each seed might affect early growth, add questions to the Driving Question Board (including 'What is seed dormancy?'), and revise their Day 1 model. Materials are local: maize grains, beans (rosecoco/Mwitemania/Wairimu), hand lenses or none, razor blades or knives, water, and printed or hand-drawn diagrams. No electricity or internet is needed; the time-lapse is recalled from Lesson 1 or replaced by the teacher's drawn sequence on the board.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the farmer who planted maize and beans on the same day after rain. Individually they write in their books: (1) in their own words, what 'growth' and 'development' mean in the seedlings they saw, and (2) a quick sketch of what they think is inside a maize grain and a bean seed before germination. They pair up, compare, then share with the class. Learners also list one thing they predict is the same and one thing different between the two seeds.
framework.teacherMoves: Display on the board (or recall orally) the time-lapse still images from Lesson 1; if no projector, draw the sequence of a bean and a maize seedling. Say: 'Think quietly for 2 minutes. Write what growth means and what development means. Then sketch the inside of a maize grain and a bean.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Is a seedling getting taller the same as a seedling forming leaves?' Circulate and note ideas. Cold-call 4 pairs: 'Pair 3, what did you decide growth means?' Record all ideas on the board without correcting. Say: 'We will test these ideas with real seeds today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share and Predict-Observe-Explain (the Predict step). Individual thinking surfaces each learner's prior ideas before they see evidence; pairing lets them rehearse scientific language; recording predictions gives a baseline to compare with observations later in the lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: Does the learner write a definition in their own words? Does the sketch show any internal parts (seed coat, embryo, food store)? Listen for misconceptions such as 'growth and development are the same thing', 'seeds are empty inside' or 'growth means only getting taller'. Tally how many of the 4 cold-called pairs mention increase in size versus change in form.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4-5 (sharing materials), learners receive soaked maize grains and soaked bean seeds. Step 1: Observe the outside with a hand lens or the naked eye, noting colour, shape, scar (hilum), small pore (micropyle) in beans, and the fused fruit wall and seed coat in maize. Step 2: Carefully split the bean along its curved edge and cut the maize grain lengthwise through the flat side. Step 3: Identify the testa, two cotyledons, plumule and radicle in the bean; pericarp/testa fused, endosperm, scutellum (single cotyledon), embryo (plumule with coleoptile, radicle with coleorhiza) in maize. Step 4: Draw large, labelled diagrams of both seeds with a title, magnification note and label lines. Step 5: Test for food stores by placing a drop of iodine solution (or diluted tincture of iodine from a pharmacy) on cut surfaces; starch turns blue-black, showing where food is stored (endosperm in maize, cotyledons in bean). Where iodine is unavailable, note the whitish floury texture of the endosperm versus the thick fleshy cotyledons. The reading provided by the teacher is used to confirm the names of parts. Learners link observations to the farmer's field: which seed parts will push out first and where the food comes from during emergence.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute pre-soaked seeds (prepared 12-24 hours earlier) and demonstrate the cut once, then say: 'Cut on the board, away from your fingers, one cutter per group.' Remind: 'Do not taste the seeds, and wash hands afterwards.' Ask while circulating: 'What do you see on the inside of the bean that you cannot see in the maize?' and 'Where do you think the baby plant is?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Cold-call 3 groups to point to the radicle and plumule on their specimen. Prompt struggling groups: 'Use the reading to match each part to its name.' Check drawings: 'Use a sharp pencil, single lines, no shading; label lines should not cross.' Use simple English and clarify terms: cotyledon = seed leaf, endosperm = food store tissue, plumule = shoot, radicle = root. For large classes, assign roles: cutter, reader, recorder, drawer, reporter, and rotate.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe step). Learners compare real structures with their earlier sketches, which creates cognitive conflict where predictions were wrong. Drawing and labelling forces careful attention to detail; roles support Unity by making each member accountable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: Cuts the seed safely and correctly? Identifies at least 4 structures in each seed? Labels radicle and plumule correctly? Records one similarity and one difference between the seeds? Oral probing: 'Which part will become the root? Which will become the shoot?' Note misconceptions such as 'the cotyledon is the leaf of the plant above ground' or 'maize has no food store'.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups complete a comparison table of monocot (maize) and dicot (bean) seeds: number of cotyledons, location of food store, seed coat, protective sheaths, and function of each structure (e.g., testa protects the embryo, micropyle allows water entry, hilum shows the point of attachment, cotyledons store/absorb food, endosperm stores starch, scutellum absorbs digested food from the endosperm, coleoptile protects the plumule as it pushes through the soil, coleorhiza protects the radicle). Using Think-Pair-Share, learners discuss: 'How might the different food stores and protective structures affect how fast and how well maize and beans emerge from the soil?' Then they write a short Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement, for example: Claim - maize and bean seeds are built differently; Evidence - our drawings show one cotyledon and a large endosperm in maize, two large cotyledons in bean; Reasoning - the position of the food store and protective sheaths affects how food reaches the embryo and how the shoot emerges. Learners also revisit their Predict definitions and rewrite them: growth = permanent increase in size, dry mass or cell number; development = changes in form and function, such as cell differentiation and formation of leaves, roots and flowers. They give Kenyan examples: a maize seedling becoming taller (growth) and later forming a tassel and cobs (development).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Turn to your partner and explain one function of a seed structure using evidence from your specimen.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 5 learners: 'Amina, what is the job of the coleoptile? What did you see that tells you this?' Press for evidence: 'How do you know?' Introduce the Gallery Walk: groups post drawings; each group visits 2 other displays with sticky notes for 'One thing that is clear' and 'One thing to improve'. Close the walk by asking: 'What did you see in another group's drawing that made you change your own?' Clarify: 'Growth and development often happen together but are not the same: a mandazi dough can increase in size but does not develop new organs.' Confirm the correct definitions only after learners have shared their reasoning.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning, Think-Pair-Share and Gallery Walk. CER links observations to explanations; Gallery Walk exposes learners to alternative drawings and corrects errors through peer review, supporting Learning to Learn.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review using a checklist: title present, label lines straight, all key parts labelled, correct function stated. Listen for CER quality: Does the claim match the evidence? Is the reasoning linked to function? Quick 3-question quiz (oral or written): (1) Name the part that becomes the root. (2) Where is food stored in maize? (3) Give one example of growth and one of development in beans. Record the number correct to identify who needs reteaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the driving question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' Each group writes on sticky notes (a) what they learned today about the seed structure and meaning of growth and development, and (b) new questions, such as 'Why do some healthy-looking seeds not germinate?', 'Does the seed coat stop water entering?', 'What is seed dormancy?'. They place notes under categories such as 'Seed structure', 'Conditions for germination', 'Dormancy', 'Growth'. Each learner completes an exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. What do we now know that we did not know yesterday? What new question do you have?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to read their questions aloud. Highlight the question 'What is seed dormancy?': 'Some of the farmer's seeds did not germinate even though they looked healthy. Could the seed itself be the reason? We will investigate this in our next lesson.' If no board space, use a manila paper chart or a chalkboard section. Collect exit tickets for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning using the Driving Question Board. Linking each day's evidence to the central phenomenon helps learners see the unit as a coherent storyline and gives ownership of next steps through learner-generated questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket success criteria: names at least one piece of evidence (e.g., 'maize has one cotyledon and endosperm; bean has two cotyledons') and links it to the driving question (e.g., 'different food stores may cause different emergence'). Check that at least two groups generate a question about why healthy seeds fail to germinate. Oral probing: 'Which of our questions can the seed structure alone answer, and which need more investigation?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Day 1 drawing or explanation of why maize and beans behave differently. Individually they revise it, adding labelled diagrams of the seed structures and a short explanation of how growth and development begin from the embryo using the stored food. They add arrows showing food moving from endosperm (maize) or cotyledons (bean) to the embryo, and a question mark for 'unknown factors' (dormancy, water, oxygen, temperature) to be tested later. They write one sentence beginning 'Before I thought..., now I think... because...'. Volunteers share revised models with a partner for a quick peer check.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Day 1 model. Using a different colour pen, add what you learned today. Show the seed parts and where the food comes from.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before asking: 'What did you change and why?' Cold-call 3 learners to share their changes. Point out gaps: 'Does your model explain why some healthy seeds did not germinate? What is missing?' Collect models for review. Assign optional homework: bring a labelled sketch of a seed from home (e.g., sukuma wiki, tomato, or kidney bean) and read about seed dormancy.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision. Using a different colour pen makes learning visible and lets learners and the teacher see how understanding changes with evidence. The remaining gaps motivate the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check: Does the revised model include correctly labelled seed structures? Does it show the stored food supplying the embryo? Does it identify at least one unanswered factor? Look for the 'Before I thought... now I think... because...' statement with an evidence-based reason. Provide feedback to those still confusing growth with development.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still treat growth and development as the same thing, and which seed structures were most often mislabelled (e.g., coleoptile vs plumule)? Did groups share cutting tools and materials fairly, and was the soaking time sufficient for easy dissection? How well did learners use evidence from their own specimens rather than textbook memory in their CER statements? Which DQB questions show readiness for dormancy, and who needs extra support with scientific English terms before Lesson 3?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed and dissected soaked maize grains and bean seeds, and saw that maize has one cotyledon (scutellum) with a large endosperm and protective coleoptile and coleorhiza, while beans have two large cotyledons, a testa, hilum, micropyle, plumule and radicle.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Growth is a permanent increase in size, dry mass or cell number, while development is the change in form and function as cells differentiate. Seed structures have specific functions such as protection, food storage, absorbing water and forming the new root and shoot.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Maize and beans are built differently, so they store and supply food to the embryo in different ways, which may partly explain differences in emergence and early growth. Since some healthy-looking seeds still failed to germinate, other factors, such as seed dormancy, must also be investigated.

LESSONS.title: Seed Dormancy: Why Do Some Healthy-Looking Seeds Refuse to Germinate?
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (single period; the dormancy-breaking set-up is started in the lesson and observed over the following days)
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: seed dormancy, impermeable seed coat, scarification, stratification, inhibitors, immature embryo, after-ripening, imbibition, germination, maize, beans, Khan Academy

slo.purpose: Learners examine seed specimens to identify causes of seed dormancy and carry out simple activities to break dormancy, so that they can explain why some seeds planted on the same day after the same rain germinate quickly, slowly or not at all.
slo.knowledge: c) Outline causes and ways of breaking dormancy in seeds. Learners define seed dormancy and state its significance (survival through dry seasons, spreading germination over time). Learners outline causes: hard or impermeable seed coat, immature embryo, presence of chemical inhibitors, and absence of the right light or temperature cues. Learners outline ways of breaking dormancy: scarification (nicking, rubbing, soaking in warm water), leaching of inhibitors, stratification or chilling, and after-ripening.
slo.skills: Observing and examining seed specimens (hand lens); asking questions; planning and carrying out a simple investigation (NGSS SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations); constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (NGSS SEP: Constructing Explanations); communicating observations in simple, clear scientific English; collaborating in small groups.
slo.attitudes: Unity: works harmoniously with others while carrying out activities. Learning to Learn: reflects on own work and adjusts accordingly while carrying out activities to demonstrate ways of breaking seed dormancy. Appreciates that farmers in Kenya depend on understanding seed behaviour to plan planting and increase yields.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Lesson 3 focus: What causes some seeds to remain dormant, and how can dormancy be broken so germination occurs?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-2 established that seeds differ in structure (monocot maize versus dicot bean) and that growth begins from the embryo inside the seed. This lesson explains one reason why seeds planted together do not behave alike: some are dormant even though they look healthy. It answers part of the driving question (why some seeds fail or delay germination) and raises the next question: How does germination occur once dormancy is broken?
slo.safetyNotes: Use only seeds not treated with pesticide (many commercial seed packets are dyed and chemically treated, so wash hands after handling, and never taste seeds). Use warm, not boiling, water, handled only by the teacher or a designated group member. Use sandpaper or a file on seeds held firmly on the bench, and keep blades and razors away from learners; nicking is done with a nail file or sandpaper. Wash hands after the practical and do not eat any seeds used in the experiment.

LESSONS.overview: Return to the anchoring phenomenon: a farmer in Molo plants maize and beans on the same day after the first rains. Most germinate in a few days, some take longer, and some healthy-looking seeds never sprout. Learners predict why, then examine seed specimens (maize, beans, and other locally available seeds such as cowpeas, pigeon peas, Acacia or Croton seeds, and avocado or pawpaw seeds if available) to look for features that might block germination. They watch the Khan Academy video 'Seed dormancy | Plant growth and development | Biology' where connectivity allows, or use the teacher-prepared alternative (a teacher-read passage with a labelled chalkboard diagram). In small groups they set up simple dormancy-breaking treatments (control, rubbing with sandpaper, warm-water soak, and cold or leaching treatment) using locally available materials. They use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning to explain what causes dormancy and add evidence to the Driving Question Board, ending with the new question: How does germination occur?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the phenomenon: maize and beans planted together after rain in Molo, yet some seeds germinate within days, some take longer, and some healthy-looking ones never germinate. Using Think-Pair-Share, each learner writes a prediction in their notebook: 'Why might a healthy-looking seed fail to germinate even when it has rain? What could we do to make it germinate?' Learners sketch one seed and mark where they think the problem might be (seed coat, embryo, inside the seed). They pair up and then share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Display on the board: 'Same day. Same rain. Different results. Why?' Say: 'Think quietly for one minute. Write your prediction and draw the seed with an arrow to the part you think is responsible.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds of silence after posing the question before accepting any answers. Move around and look at the drawings. Say: 'Turn to your partner and explain your idea in simple English. Partner, ask: What makes you think so?' Cold-call 4 pairs, including at least 2 who have not spoken in the previous lessons. Record all predictions on the board under the heading 'Our predictions' without judging them (for example: 'seed is dead', 'no water', 'seed coat is too hard', 'seed is still sleeping'). Say: 'Today we will test these ideas with real seeds.' Introduce the word 'dormancy' as 'a resting state where a living seed does not germinate even when conditions look right'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share and Predict-Observe-Explain (the Predict step): Individual thinking commits each learner to an idea before evidence is seen, pair talk lets learners rehearse scientific English, and recording predictions publicly creates ideas the class can later confirm or revise. This ties directly to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each learner's notebook has a written prediction and an annotated seed drawing. (2) Count learners who locate the cause at the seed coat, the embryo, or only 'lack of water'. (3) Listen for misconceptions such as 'a seed that does not germinate is dead' or 'all seeds germinate immediately if watered'. Tally these on a quick checklist for use in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (10 min): In groups of 4-5 (sharing hand lenses and specimens), learners examine seed specimens: maize grains, bean seeds, cowpeas, and any hard-coated local seeds available (for example Acacia, Senna/Cassia, Croton, Grevillea or avocado seeds). They feel the hardness, observe the seed coat with a hand lens, and compare the coat thickness of a dry seed with a seed that has been soaked. They record observations in a table: seed type, coat description (thin/thick, smooth/hard), water uptake after soaking (swells or not). They then watch the Khan Academy video on seed dormancy (or hear the teacher-read alternative) and note causes of dormancy. Part B (10 min): Groups carry out activities to demonstrate ways of breaking seed dormancy. Each group sets up 4 labelled containers (cut plastic bottles or clay saucers lined with wet cotton wool, cloth or paper towel) with 5-6 hard-coated seeds each (for example Senna, Acacia, or old bean seeds): (1) control - untreated seeds, (2) scarification - seed coat rubbed lightly on sandpaper or a rough stone, (3) warm-water soak - seeds soaked in warm (not boiling) water for a few hours, (4) leaching/chilling - seeds washed in several changes of water or kept in a cool place. All containers are kept moist and placed in the same location, and groups record observations daily.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the lesson, prepare per group: seed samples in small cups, one hand lens (or share between two groups), sandpaper strips, warm water in a flask, cotton wool or cloth, 4 containers (cut plastic bottles), labels, and pencils. If connectivity is available, play the Khan Academy video 'Seed dormancy | Plant growth and development | Biology' once on a projector or the teacher's phone with the class gathered around it; pause twice to ask 'What is stopping this seed from germinating?' with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking responses. If there is no connectivity, use the teacher-prepared alternative: read aloud a 150-word passage and draw a labelled diagram on the board showing a hard seed coat, inhibitors, and an immature embryo. Say: 'Hold the seed. Is the coat hard? Does water enter? Write what you SEE, not what you think.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which seed took up water fastest? Why do you think so?' and 'What is your control and why do we need it?' Cold-call 3 groups to report one observation each. Remind groups: 'Warm water only, not boiling, and wash hands after handling seeds.' Assign roles (materials manager, recorder, timekeeper, reporter) to support unity and fair participation. Where the class is large, groups can share sandpaper and flasks.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the Observe step): Learners collect firsthand evidence about seed coats, water uptake and treatment effects, which they will later compare with their predictions. The control group enables fair comparison, and group roles and shared materials build Unity while keeping the practical feasible for large classes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use an observation checklist per group with these indicators: (1) handles seeds safely and correctly uses the hand lens; (2) records at least two observable seed-coat features; (3) sets up all four containers correctly with labels and a control; (4) every member has a role and takes part; (5) uses precise words such as 'hard', 'swollen', 'absorbed' in simple scientific English. Use oral probes: 'How do you know the water entered the seed?' and 'Why must the amount of water be the same in all containers?' to identify misconceptions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) to answer: 'What causes seed dormancy, and how can it be broken?' On a sheet or in their notebooks, each group writes a Claim (for example 'A hard seed coat prevents water from entering, so the seed remains dormant'), supports it with Evidence from the seed examinations and the video (for example 'The Senna seeds did not swell after soaking, but the rubbed seeds did'), and gives Reasoning linking it to biology (water uptake, called imbibition, activates enzymes in the embryo; the coat blocks water and gas entry; inhibitors must be removed or broken down). Learners then link causes of dormancy to the farmer's field: why might some bean seeds delay in the soil? They also discuss the significance of dormancy for plants in Kenyan ecosystems, such as seeds of Acacia in the Tsavo drylands waiting for adequate rain.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use the CER frame: My claim is... My evidence is... This is because...' Display the frame on the board. Pose: 'Why did the control seeds behave differently from the rubbed seeds?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 4 groups to share their CER aloud, and ask a different learner in the group to defend it, not the recorder. Probe: 'What other cause of dormancy could explain a seed that is healthy but still does not germinate?' (guide towards inhibitors, immature embryo, and temperature/light cues). Clarify tricky terms on the board: dormancy, scarification, imbibition, inhibitor, embryo. Connect to the phenomenon: 'How could this explain why some of the farmer's seeds did not germinate after the same rain?' Address misconceptions flagged in the Predict phase, for example 'Not germinating does not always mean dead; the seed may be dormant.' Summarise the causes (hard seed coat, chemical inhibitors, immature embryo, environmental cues) and the ways of breaking dormancy (scarification, soaking, leaching, chilling/stratification, after-ripening), and mention farmers' practices such as soaking bean or pigeon pea seeds overnight, or cracking hard seeds slightly before planting.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): Learners are required to connect each claim to evidence from their own observations and to scientific reasoning, moving from describing seeds to explaining why they behave differently. Discussion and questioning reveal gaps and confirm correct ideas, and linking back to the farmer's field makes the explanation relevant to the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a CER check with these indicators: (1) the claim is a clear statement about the cause of dormancy; (2) at least one piece of evidence comes from the class observations, not only the video; (3) the reasoning mentions water or gas entry, inhibitors, or embryo development; (4) learners correct the misconception that non-germinating seeds are always dead. Peer-review CER statements by swapping with another group and giving one star (good point) and one wish (improvement). The teacher notes groups needing reteaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class Driving Question Board: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' In their groups they write new sticky notes or strips of paper with (a) one thing they now know (for example 'Hard seed coats can block water and cause dormancy') and (b) one new question (for example 'What happens inside the seed once water enters?' or 'How does the seed know when to start growing?'). They post these on the board and group them under headings such as 'Causes of delay or failure' and 'What happens during germination'. Learners also move any earlier question that has now been answered into an 'Answered' section.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk to the board with one note that shows what we have learned today and one that shows what we still wonder.' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds for learners to think before writing. Cold-call 3 learners to read their notes aloud and justify where they placed them. Highlight the question 'How does germination occur?' and say: 'This is our next step. Once dormancy is broken, what exactly happens in the seed?' Ask: 'Which of our earlier questions about maize and beans can we now partly answer?' Move 2-3 questions to the 'Answered' section with learners' agreement, citing the evidence. Keep the DQB visible in the classroom, and remind learners to watch the dormancy set-ups daily.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning using the Driving Question Board: Learners see how each lesson's evidence contributes to the main question, track what is answered or unanswered, and generate the next investigation question themselves, so learning is purposeful and connected.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each group posts at least one 'know' note and one 'wonder' note; (2) notes use evidence from today's work, not just recall; (3) at least one question leads naturally to germination (for example the process, the role of water, oxygen or temperature); (4) learners can explain why they placed a note in a certain category. Record the quality of questions on the observation checklist.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their Day 1 drawing and explanation of why the farmer's seeds behave differently. Individually, they revise it by adding a labelled sketch of a dormant seed showing the hard seed coat, inhibitors, and embryo, and arrows showing how scarification or soaking allows water to enter. They add a short note: 'New idea: Some seeds fail to germinate because ______, and farmers can help by ______.' In pairs, they swap drawings and give one piece of peer feedback. Before leaving, each learner completes an exit ticket answering: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Day 1 model. Using a different colour pen, add what you have learned about dormancy. Show cause and solution.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after giving the instruction before circulating, so learners start thinking independently. Walk around and ask 3-4 learners: 'What did you add and what evidence made you change it?' Cold-call 2 pairs to share a revision and the evidence behind it. Say: 'Place your revised model in your portfolio. Over the next few days we will check our containers and add more evidence.' Hand out or write the exit ticket questions on the board and collect them at the door. Remind groups to keep their dormancy set-ups in a safe, shaded spot, to keep the cotton or cloth moist, and to record daily observations (this supports the later Gallery Walk of germination results). Announce the next lesson: 'How does germination occur?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: Learners compare their earlier thinking with new evidence and make visible changes to their model, showing conceptual growth. Peer review and exit tickets strengthen reflection (Learning to Learn) and show how today's evidence connects to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check indicators: (1) the revised drawing includes a labelled seed coat, embryo and inhibitors; (2) at least one cause of dormancy and one method of breaking it are shown with arrows or notes; (3) a change from the Day 1 model is clearly visible; (4) the exit ticket cites specific evidence (for example 'rubbed seeds swelled but untreated seeds did not') and links it to why some seeds in the farmer's field did not germinate. Use a quick quiz of 3 questions at the start of the next lesson on causes and ways of breaking dormancy.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Which misconceptions about non-germinating seeds persisted (for example 'dormant means dead')? Were group roles effective in ensuring that every learner handled seeds and contributed ideas? Did the large class size limit hand-lens use or sandpaper sharing, and how can materials be organised better? Did learners use the CER structure with real evidence from their containers, or mostly the video? Was the teacher-prepared alternative needed, and was it as clear as the video? What indicators on the checklist show that learners are ready for the germination lesson? Plan to check the set-ups over the next days and use the results in the Gallery Walk.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We examined maize, bean and other local seeds with hand lenses, noting hard and thin seed coats and how much water the seeds absorbed. We set up control, scarified, warm-water-soaked and leached/chilled seeds and recorded changes over time.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Seed dormancy is a resting state in which a living seed fails to germinate even when conditions seem suitable. Causes include a hard impermeable seed coat, chemical inhibitors, an immature embryo, and unsuitable environmental cues. Dormancy can be broken by scarification, soaking in warm water, leaching, chilling (stratification) and after-ripening. Dormancy helps seeds survive unfavourable seasons and spreads germination over time.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Some seeds in the farmer's field do not germinate or are delayed even after the same rain because they are dormant: their hard seed coats may block water entry, inhibitors may need to be washed away or broken down, or their embryos may not be ready. Evidence: in our containers, treated seeds took up water and responded sooner than untreated controls. This explains part of the difference in germination between maize and beans, but we still need to find out how germination occurs once dormancy is broken.

LESSONS.title: Germination: Process, Types and Conditions Necessary for Germination in Maize and Bean Seeds
LESSONS.duration: 80 minutes (double period); set-up in lesson, observations continue over 5-7 days in 5-minute slots
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: germination, hypogeal, epigeal, water, oxygen, suitable temperature, viability, control, variable, cotyledon, radicle, plumule, maize, beans

slo.purpose: Learners investigate the conditions necessary for germination and the types of germination (hypogeal and epigeal) using maize and bean seeds, so they can explain why seeds planted on the same day after the same rain germinate and emerge differently.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (d) investigate conditions necessary for seed germination, and (e) investigate types of germination in plants. They outline the process of germination (water uptake, activation of enzymes, radicle emergence, then plumule), and distinguish hypogeal germination (maize, which keeps cotyledons below the soil) from epigeal germination (common bean, where cotyledons are lifted above the soil).
slo.skills: Predicting, planning a fair test and identifying variables (SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations); recording and comparing observations; constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (SEP: Constructing Explanations); communicating in clear scientific English. Core competency: Learning to Learn, where the learner reflects on their own work and adjusts accordingly.
slo.attitudes: Unity: the learner works harmoniously with others while carrying out experiments to investigate conditions necessary for seed germination. Curiosity and respect for evidence when results differ from predictions. Appreciation of the importance of growth and development in plants (outcome h).
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Lesson focus: What conditions and processes must be in place before a seed can begin to grow, and how do maize and beans differ as they emerge?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-3 established seed structure and dormancy. Lesson 4 gathers evidence for the first part of the phenomenon: why seeds planted together after the same rain germinate at different times, or fail even when they look healthy. Learners find that water alone is not enough, since oxygen, suitable temperature and a viable, non-dormant seed are also needed, and that maize and beans emerge differently. This raises the next question: once the seedling has emerged, How do plants show growth?
slo.safetyNotes: Use only clean, untreated seeds. Do NOT use seed maize or bean seed treated with pesticide (often pink or red dyed from agrovets). If treated seed is the only supply, the teacher handles it and learners wear gloves, and it is not used for eating. Wash hands after handling seeds, soil and wet cotton or tissue. Do not taste any seeds. Boil water only under teacher control, then cool it fully before use. Keep a heat source away from learner benches. Clear spilt water immediately to prevent slips. Dispose of mouldy seeds in a sealed bag, and learners must not sniff them closely.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the anchoring phenomenon of the farmer who plants maize and beans on the same day after rain, yet sees uneven germination, delayed emergence and some failed seeds. In small groups of 5-6 (suited to large classes) they predict, then set up a fair test using locally available materials (plastic cups, old jam jars, cotton wool or tissue, sawdust or soil, polythene bags, a sufuria, a cold place such as a wet cloth in a shaded clay pot or fridge if available): Set A with water, air and warmth (control); Set B dry seeds; Set C seeds submerged in boiled, cooled water with oil on top (little oxygen); Set D cold or cool conditions; and Set E boiled (non-viable) seeds. Maize and bean seeds are used in each set. Set-up takes about 30 minutes and groups observe for 5-7 days. To gather evidence on the same day, learners also examine pre-germinated seeds (teacher-prepared 4-6 days before) of maize and beans, drawing and comparing hypogeal and epigeal germination. If a time-lapse video is available it is shown on a phone or projector; otherwise the teacher uses a prepared picture sequence or flip chart. Learners use Predict-Observe-Explain, Think-Pair-Share and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning, then add questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their Day 1 model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the phenomenon: a farmer in Molo plants maize and beans on the same day after the first rains; some seeds sprout in 4 days, some in 10, and some healthy-looking seeds never sprout. Individually, they write a prediction in their notebooks: 'Which conditions does a seed need to germinate? What will happen to maize and bean seeds in: (a) dry air, (b) water with no air, (c) cold, (d) warm, moist, open air?' They sketch what they expect to see after 5 days and give one reason. They then pair up (Think-Pair-Share) and compare. Finally, groups agree on a group prediction chart for the 5 set-ups, listing the variable they will change and the ones they must keep the same.
framework.teacherMoves: Display or read the phenomenon: 'A farmer in Molo plants maize and beans on the same day, under the same rain. Why might some seeds sprout quickly, some slowly and some not at all?' Say: 'Think quietly and write your own prediction. You have 2 minutes. No talking yet.' Then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking 'What does a seed need before it can start growing?' before taking any answer. Say: 'Turn to your partner. Share your prediction and tell them WHY you think so.' Circulate and listen for misconceptions such as 'seeds need soil to germinate' or 'seeds need light to germinate'. Cold-call 4 pairs: 'Amina and Otieno, what did your partner predict, and what was the reason?' Record all predictions on the board without judging. Ask: 'Which prediction could we test? How would we make the test fair?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Predict step) and Think-Pair-Share. Committing to a written prediction before any evidence makes learners' existing ideas visible and gives them something to confront with data later. Think-Pair-Share lets every learner, including quiet ones in a large class, rehearse an explanation before speaking publicly, which builds confidence and surfaces competing ideas for investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: (1) learner writes a prediction with a reason, not just a guess; (2) learner mentions at least one condition (water, air or oxygen, warmth); (3) learner can state what would be kept the same. Oral probing: 'Why do you think soil is needed?' to identify the misconception that soil, light or fertiliser is essential for germination. Teacher tallies on the board how many pairs predicted that each condition is necessary. Learners who give only 'water' are noted for follow-up questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (about 30 min): Groups set up the fair test. Each of 5 labelled containers receives 5 maize and 5 bean seeds on moist cotton wool or tissue: A = moist, open to air, room temperature (control); B = dry cotton, no water; C = seeds fully submerged in boiled and cooled water with a thin layer of cooking oil on top (little oxygen); D = moist, in a cool place (wet cloth in a shaded clay pot, or a fridge if the school has one); E = boiled-then-cooled seeds on moist cotton (non-viable seeds). Groups label, draw the set-up and make a results table (day, number germinated, radicle length in mm, notes). Part B (about 25 min): Groups examine teacher-prepared germinating maize and bean seedlings (started 4-6 days earlier) and, if available, watch a 2-minute time-lapse. They draw and label both: maize with the coleoptile and plumule emerging while the cotyledon stays below ground (hypogeal), and bean with the hypocotyl arching and lifting the cotyledons above the soil (epigeal). Part C (5-7 days): Groups record observations in 5-minute daily slots.
framework.teacherMoves: Give out materials in advance in trays for each group (one tray per 5-6 learners). Say: 'Roles today: materials manager, recorder, timekeeper, reporter, and safety officer. Everyone handles the seeds at least once.' Demonstrate one set-up for 2 minutes, then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which condition are we changing in Container C, and which ones must stay the same?' Cold-call 3 groups to state their variable. Circulate with prompts: 'What are you measuring? How will you count a seed as germinated?' 'Why are we using 5 seeds of each type instead of 1?' For Part B, ask: 'Where is the cotyledon in the maize seedling? Where is it in the bean?' WAIT 10-15 seconds before accepting answers. If no electricity or data, hold up a prepared chart or sketch sequence of the time-lapse. Teacher prepares a spare container of already-germinated seeds in case some groups' set-ups fail. Remind: 'Unity: share equipment fairly and listen to every group member's ideas.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe step). Learners test their predictions with controlled variables, so they see that any difference in germination can be linked to one condition. Comparing maize and bean seedlings side by side helps them describe types of germination from evidence rather than memory, and connects directly to the phenomenon of why the two crops emerge differently.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist with indicators: (1) group labels every container and identifies the changed variable; (2) all members handle materials and take turns; (3) measurements are recorded with units (mm) and dates; (4) drawings show correct labelled parts (radicle, plumule, cotyledon, coleoptile, hypocotyl); (5) learner correctly tells which seed is hypogeal and which is epigeal. Oral probe: 'Why do we include dry seeds and boiled seeds?' Note groups that confuse 'germination' with 'growth' for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners meet after the first results (day 3-5) and use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning to answer: 'What conditions are necessary for maize and bean seeds to germinate, and how do the two seed types differ in emergence?' Each group writes a claim, cites evidence from its table (e.g., 'In A, 9 of 10 seeds germinated by day 4; in B, 0 of 10'), and gives reasoning in terms of biology: water activates enzymes and softens the seed coat, oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration to release energy, and suitable temperature allows enzymes to work. They explain why boiled seeds failed (embryo dead, so not viable) and link back to the phenomenon: healthy-looking seeds that failed could be dead, dormant, waterlogged (low oxygen) or too cold or dry. They then hold a Gallery Walk: groups post their CER and labelled drawings, and visit other groups' work to give one 'star' (strength) and one 'wish' (suggestion).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your results tables. Write your claim first, then your evidence, then your reasoning. Use the sentence starter: I claim that ... because the data show ... which happens because ...'. Ask: 'In Container C there was water but few seeds germinated. What does that tell you?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Press for reasoning: 'Which biological process needs oxygen? Why would waterlogged shamba soils in Kisumu affect maize seed?' Connect: 'Why might the farmer's seeds in the dry patch of the field fail, and the ones in a flooded patch near Lake Victoria also fail?' Prompt on dormancy: 'Some seeds were in good conditions but didn't germinate. What from Lesson 3 could explain this?' For the Gallery Walk, give 8 minutes and a timer: 'Move clockwise every 2 minutes. Leave one star and one wish on a sticky note or a piece of paper.' Clarify terms in simple English: 'hypogeal means below ground; epigeal means above ground.' Correct misconceptions with evidence, not telling.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a Gallery Walk. CER forces learners to separate what they observed from the scientific explanation, reducing guessing. Gallery Walk exposes them to other groups' data, including results that may differ, which teaches that evidence from many trials strengthens a claim and encourages peer review.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a CER rubric: Claim (clear, testable, matches question); Evidence (specific numbers or observations from the table); Reasoning (links evidence to a biological principle such as respiration, enzymes or water uptake). Exit-level indicators: learner states at least 3 conditions (water, oxygen, suitable temperature) and one internal factor (viable, non-dormant seed); learner correctly classifies maize as hypogeal and bean as epigeal with a structural reason. Peer review: stars and wishes are collected and checked by the teacher. Oral probing identifies the misconception that 'seeds need light or soil to germinate.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the main question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' In groups, they write on sticky notes or paper strips: (1) one thing we now know about germination (with evidence), and (2) one new question. Examples: 'Why do bean cotyledons rise but maize ones stay?', 'Why did some seeds in A germinate later than others?', 'How do plants show growth after the seedling emerges?' They place notes under headings: Germination conditions, Types of germination, Growth after emergence, Unanswered. They complete an exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which of today's findings help answer the driving question? Which parts are still a mystery?' After asking 'Which question on the board can we answer next?' give WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups to read one new question and say where to place it. Group questions with learners, highlighting the question: 'Our seedlings have emerged, but how do plants show growth? How would we measure it?' Tell learners: 'That is our focus in the next lesson.' Collect exit tickets as learners leave. If no stickies are available, use torn exercise-book paper and masking tape or chalk-drawn columns on the blackboard.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning using the Driving Question Board. Linking each new finding to the central question keeps learning coherent, shows how evidence builds toward an explanation, and turns learners' unanswered questions into the direction of the unit. Learners see that science advances through questions generated by evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket indicators: (1) names specific evidence such as 'Seeds in dry cotton did not germinate'; (2) links the evidence to the driving question; (3) writes at least one productive new question.
