Teacher sorts tickets into three piles: secure, partial, and misconception (e.g., 'seeds need sunlight to germinate') and plans a quick re-teach at the start of Lesson 5. Observe DQB placements for accuracy.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Day 1 drawings and explanations of the phenomenon. Individually, they revise the model by adding: (a) the conditions needed to germinate (water, oxygen, suitable temperature, viable and non-dormant seed) shown with arrows; (b) a labelled diagram of maize (hypogeal) and bean (epigeal) germination; and (c) a short note answering: 'Why might the farmer's seeds, planted together after the same rain, germinate at different times or fail?' They use a different colour pen for revisions so that changes are visible. They swap with a partner for peer review using the prompt: 'What evidence supports each new part of the model? What is still missing?' They leave a space labelled 'What happens after emergence?' to complete in Lesson 5.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take your Day 1 model. Use a different colour to add what you now know. Every addition should be backed by evidence from our containers.' Circulate and ask: 'Where did you get this idea? Which container shows it?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before following up. Cold-call 3 learners to describe one change they made and why. Pair review for 5 minutes: 'Give your partner one suggestion and one strength.' Say: 'Keep your model safe; we will add growth next.' Collect a sample of 5-6 models for checking. Remind groups to observe containers for the remaining days and record data.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision. Revisiting the Day 1 model with a new colour makes learning visible to the learner and the teacher. Linking each change to evidence shows how scientific models are improved, and it prompts learners to identify gaps (growth after emergence) that the next investigations will fill.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check indicators: (1) at least three conditions for germination are added with arrows or labels; (2) hypogeal and epigeal types are drawn and labelled correctly (cotyledons below or above soil); (3) revisions are linked to evidence; (4) the explanation addresses why seeds planted together behave differently (viability, dormancy, uneven moisture, oxygen or temperature); (5) peer feedback is specific. Note learners who still hold misconceptions for individual conferencing.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners distinguish between germination and growth? Which groups could name the variable they changed and the ones kept constant? Did any learners still believe that seeds need soil or light to germinate, and what evidence changed their minds? Were the materials sufficient for the class size, and did group roles ensure everyone participated? Were the seed set-ups reliable (check for mould, drying out, or treated seed)? Did the pre-germinated seedlings arrive on time? How well did learners use CER with specific numbers? What adjustments are needed before Lesson 5 to measure growth, such as preparing extra seedlings, rulers and string, and a recording table? Also record which learners need extra support with English scientific vocabulary.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We set up maize and bean seeds in containers with different conditions (moist and open to air, dry, submerged with little oxygen, cool, and boiled seeds) and compared them over several days. We also examined and drew germinating maize and bean seedlings. Record the number of seeds germinated in each container and the differences between how the maize and bean seedlings emerged.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate, and they must be alive (viable) and not dormant. Germination starts with water uptake, then the radicle emerges, then the plumule. Maize shows hypogeal germination (cotyledon stays below ground), while bean shows epigeal germination (cotyledons are lifted above ground).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Seeds planted on the same day after the same rain can germinate at different times, or fail, because of differences in moisture, oxygen (for example in waterlogged soil), temperature, seed viability and dormancy. Maize and beans also emerge differently because of their type of germination. After emergence, how do plants show growth? This will be investigated in the next lesson.

LESSONS.title: Primary and Secondary Growth: How Do Plants Show Growth?
LESSONS.duration: 80 minutes (double period) – can be split into 40 + 40 minutes
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: primary growth, secondary growth, apical meristem, vascular cambium, cork cambium, xylem, phloem, monocot stem, dicot stem, annual rings, hypogeal, epigeal, growth, Think-Pair-Share, CER

slo.purpose: Learners gather evidence from stem sections and models to distinguish primary growth (increase in length) from secondary growth (increase in girth). They link this to the maize and bean seedlings that grew taller and thicker after germination, and to the observation that bean plants branch and thicken while maize does not.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) illustrate primary and secondary growth in flowering plants (SLO f); (2) relate the structures seen in stem sections to their functions (xylem, phloem, cambium, cortex, epidermis); (3) explain why a dicot stem such as bean or a Grevillea/Cypress tree thickens while a monocot stem such as maize mostly does not; (4) connect this to the germination types compared in earlier lessons (hypogeal in maize, epigeal in bean).
slo.skills: Observing prepared slides or photomicrographs under a light microscope; drawing and labelling stem sections with a title, scale and annotations; using models to represent stages of secondary growth; Claim-Evidence-Reasoning writing; peer review; working safely in groups. NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Unity: works harmoniously with others while sharing microscopes and materials. Learning to Learn: reflects on own drawings and models and adjusts them using peer feedback and evidence. Appreciation of the importance of growth and development in plants, including trees in school nurseries and for preventing global warming.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Question raised for this lesson: How do plants show growth?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1–4 established seed structure, dormancy, and the conditions for germination, and compared hypogeal and epigeal germination. Learners now look beyond germination to the growth that follows: why seedlings get taller and thicker, why roots go deeper, and why beans branch. This lesson adds the explanation of growth in length and girth through meristems. It ends with the new question 'How can we measure growth in plants?', leading to Lesson 6.
slo.safetyNotes: Handle microscope slides and cover slips carefully; report broken glass to the teacher and do not pick it up with bare hands. Carry microscopes with two hands. Use a sharp razor blade or knife only under teacher supervision, cutting away from the body on a firm board. Wash hands after handling plant material and soil. If microscopes are few, rotate groups of 6 at stations and use photomicrographs or teacher-drawn charts at other stations. Cutting stems are used in place of electricity-dependent resources.

LESSONS.overview: The anchoring phenomenon showed maize and bean seeds planted on the same day after rain, yet growing differently: stems getting taller and thicker, roots going deeper, and some plants branching. Today learners focus on how this growth happens. They predict which parts of a young maize and bean seedling and which parts of an old tree such as a Grevillea or Eucalyptus grow in length or girth, then observe stem sections (prepared slides, photomicrographs or hand-cut sections of young bean and maize stems) and use the reading on primary and secondary growth. They draw and label sections, build a simple plasticine or paper model of secondary growth in a woody dicot stem, and explain using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning. They add questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their class model of why maize and bean plants differ. Offline alternative: use a teacher-prepared printed chart of the stem sections and sketches drawn on the board if no microscopes are available.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the time-lapse of maize and bean seedlings. The teacher holds up a young bean seedling, a maize seedling, and a cut piece of firewood (from Eucalyptus or Cypress) showing rings. Individually learners write for 2 minutes: (a) Which parts of the seedlings are getting longer? (b) Why is the firewood stem so thick while a maize stem stays slim? (c) Where in the stem do you think new cells are made? They sketch a prediction of a cross-section of a bean stem and a maize stem, showing where growth happens. They share with a partner (Think-Pair-Share), then with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the specimens and say: "Remember our farmer's field in Molo. Same day, same rain, but look at these plants. Think quietly: where does a plant get longer and where does it get thicker?" Give 2 minutes of silent think time, then say: "Turn to your partner and compare your sketches." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before calling on anyone. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) to share, including at least 2 who predicted something different. Say: "Tell me what made you predict that." Record predictions on the board without judging. Ask: "What would we need to see to know who is right?" Clarify terms such as 'growth' and 'girth' in simple English.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with Think-Pair-Share: individual prediction exposes preconceptions (for example, that plants grow all over like animals, or that all plants thicken the same way). Pairing lets learners test ideas on a peer in low-risk talk, and the class list of predictions gives a reason for the observation phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: Does the learner write a prediction with a reason? Is the sketch showing at least one location of growth (e.g. shoot tip, root tip, between bark and wood)? Listen for misconceptions: 'plants grow from the bottom', 'thickness is just the stem stretching', 'maize and beans grow the same way'. Note names of at least 6 learners with misconceptions to revisit in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 5-6, learners rotate through 3 stations (about 8 minutes each): Station 1 – Observe a prepared slide or photomicrograph (or a hand-cut thin section stained with diluted ink or iodine) of a young dicot (bean) stem and a monocot (maize) stem under a light microscope; draw one low-power plan diagram and label epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles, xylem, phloem, and cambium (dicot only); note arrangement (ring versus scattered). Station 2 – Study a photomicrograph or chart of an older woody dicot stem showing secondary xylem, secondary phloem, vascular cambium, cork cambium, and cork, and a cut Eucalyptus/Cypress/Grevillea log showing annual rings; count rings and record. Station 3 – Read the 'primary and secondary growth' passage and fill in a table: Where? Which meristem? What increases? Examples in maize, bean, and tree. Learners record at least three observations per station in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce stations: "You are plant detectives. Your evidence will help us explain how maize and bean plants grow differently." Assign roles (microscopist, recorder, drawer, timekeeper) and rotate roles. Circulate and ask: "What do you see between the xylem and phloem?" "How is the maize stem different from the bean stem?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups at each station to describe one observation. Remind: "Draw what you see, not what you think should be there. Use a sharp pencil, a title, and label lines that do not cross." Safety reminder for razor blades and microscopes. Where there are not enough microscopes, point to photomicrographs or teacher-prepared charts. If no electricity, use natural light near a window for mirror-based microscopes. Prompt for simple English: "A ring of vascular bundles means..." Provide sentence starters.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence gathering through multiple representations (microscope view, photomicrograph, real log, reading) lets learners triangulate. Using a 'draw-and-label' approach slows observation, which builds understanding of structure–function links: cambium located between xylem and phloem is the source of new cells for girth.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: Uses microscope correctly (focuses from low to high power) – yes/no; Drawing has title, clear lines, labels with straight pointer lines; identifies ring versus scattered bundles; notes cambium in the bean stem but not in maize; counts rings correctly. Oral probing: "Where do you think new cells are being made?" Look for evidence-based answers, e.g. 'the cambium is a thin layer between the xylem and phloem'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their drawings and notes to build a simple 3-step model of secondary growth in a woody dicot (such as Grevillea in a Kericho farm): Step 1 – young stem with vascular bundles and cambium; Step 2 – cambium forms a complete ring and produces secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward; Step 3 – stem thickens, cork cambium forms cork, bark develops, annual rings appear. Learners use coloured plasticine or paper strips (or draw stages on card) to make the model. Then each group writes a CER: Claim – why do bean plants thicken and branch while maize stems stay mostly the same width? Evidence – at least two observations from stations; Reasoning – linking the presence of cambium to secondary growth, apical meristems to primary growth, and monocot vascular bundles being scattered with no cambium. They also connect to the germination types: maize (hypogeal) and beans (epigeal) both start with primary growth from the shoot and root apical meristems.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use your evidence, not just your memory. Show me where in your model the stem gets thicker." Give 5 minutes for groups to make the model, then 5 minutes for the CER. Move around and ask: "What is your evidence for that claim?" "What would happen to a Eucalyptus tree if the cambium were removed all around the stem?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups (different from the Observe phase) to read their CER. Use the 'yes, and' technique to build on answers. Address misconceptions noticed earlier, e.g. 'plants thicken by stretching'. Give a clear teacher mini-explanation if needed: primary growth = apical meristems = length; secondary growth = lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium) = girth. Ask learners to connect: "How does this help explain our farmer's maize and beans?" Hold a Gallery Walk for 8 minutes: groups leave models and CERs on desks, visit two other groups, and leave one sticky note with 'a star' (strength) and 'a wish' (suggestion).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) pushes learners to justify explanations with observations. Modelling secondary growth in stages makes an invisible process visible. The Gallery Walk with peer review exposes learners to alternative models and strengthens argumentation and Learning to Learn.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review of models and CER using a 3-point rubric: (1) Claim is clear and answers the question; (2) at least two pieces of specific evidence cited; (3) reasoning links cambium or apical meristem to growth. Teacher listens for correct use of 'primary growth', 'secondary growth', 'cambium', 'apical meristem'. Quick check: ask 5 learners to state in one sentence the difference between primary and secondary growth. Misconceptions to flag: 'all plants have secondary growth' or 'primary growth only occurs in seedlings'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the main question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' In groups they write on sticky notes: (a) one thing they now know about growth, linked to evidence, and (b) one new question, e.g. 'How can we measure how fast a bean seedling grows?', 'What makes a plant stop growing?', 'Do hormones affect how stems and branches grow?'. They place the notes under categories on the DQB (Seed structure, Germination, Growth, Hormones, Measurement). The class identifies the question for the next lesson: How can you measure growth in plants?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the DQB. Which of our questions did today's evidence help to answer?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Invite 3 learners (cold-call) to move a sticky note to 'partly answered' or 'answered' and justify using evidence. Say: "What new questions has today raised?" Cold-call 4 groups to read new questions. Highlight the one on measuring growth: "If we want to compare maize and bean growth fairly, what would we need to measure?" If the DQB is not available, use chart paper or a chalkboard section that is preserved for the unit. Encourage learners to ask questions in simple English and help rephrase where needed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the Driving Question Board links each day's evidence to the unit question and builds learner ownership. Sorting questions into categories shows how pieces of learning fit together and drives the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket (written on a half page): (1) 'What evidence did we gather today?' (2) 'How does this help answer our driving question?' (3) One question you still have. Success indicators: names at least one specific observation (e.g. cambium between xylem and phloem, rings in a log) and links it to growth in length or thickness of maize or beans. Sort tickets into 'ready', 'nearly', and 'needs support' piles to plan Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Day 1 drawings and explanations about why maize and beans differ and revise them. They add a section titled 'After germination: how the plants grow', including labelled arrows showing the shoot and root apical meristems (primary growth) and lateral meristems (secondary growth in the bean and woody plants but not in maize). They use a different coloured pen to mark changes and add a short note: 'I changed ... because the evidence showed ...'. Pairs swap books and give peer feedback with one improvement suggestion. A few volunteers present revised models to the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use a different colour pen so we can see how your thinking has grown. What did you add today and what evidence made you change your model?" Give 7 minutes for revision, then 3 minutes for peer review. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before asking pairs to share. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one change they made. Ask: "Is there anything in your model that you are not sure about yet?" Collect model checks for review and note which learners still confuse primary and secondary growth. Remind groups of the practical project: a tree nursery using stem cuttings and natural hormone sources such as onion, Aloe, and cinnamon, which will connect to growth and hormones in later lessons. Close by setting the hook: "We know plants grow in length and girth. How could we measure that? Think about how you would measure a maize seedling at home in Eldoret or Kisumu."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: learners reconstruct their explanation with new evidence, which makes learning visible and builds the habit of improving ideas with data. Using a different colour pen documents the change in thinking. Peer feedback builds scientific communication.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check using criteria: (1) The model includes primary growth at shoot and root tips; (2) includes secondary growth by cambium for dicots; (3) explains why maize stems differ from bean stems; (4) at least one change is justified with evidence. Quick quiz (3 questions): name the meristem that increases girth; state where primary growth occurs; give one example of a plant showing secondary growth. Learners scoring below 2 out of 3 get a short reteach in Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Which learners could correctly distinguish primary from secondary growth using evidence, and which still hold the misconception that plants thicken by stretching? Did the microscope stations work with limited equipment, or should more photomicrographs and log sections be used next time? Were learners able to link stem anatomy to the maize and bean phenomenon? How effective was the CER writing in simple scientific English? What adjustments are needed for the next lesson on measuring growth (for example, preparing seedlings, rulers, string, and a data table for growth curves)? Did every group member participate and share equipment fairly (Unity)? Note which exit tickets show readiness to move on.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed prepared slides, photomicrographs or hand-cut sections of young bean (dicot) and maize (monocot) stems and a cut log from a woody tree with annual rings. We saw vascular bundles in a ring in the bean stem with cambium between xylem and phloem, scattered bundles in maize with no cambium, and secondary xylem, bark and rings in the older woody stem.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that primary growth is an increase in length produced by apical meristems at shoot and root tips, while secondary growth is an increase in girth produced by the vascular cambium and cork cambium in dicots and woody plants. Maize (a monocot) mainly shows primary growth, whereas bean and trees such as Grevillea and Eucalyptus show both. This raises the question: How can you measure growth in plants?
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning, we explained that part of the difference in how maize and bean plants grow after germination is due to stem structure: the bean stem has cambium that allows thickening and branching, while the maize stem lacks cambium and grows mainly in length. This adds to our model that differences in germination and growth depend on seed structure, germination conditions, and the meristems that drive growth.

LESSONS.title: Where Does a Maize or Bean Plant Grow? Measuring Growth and Regions of Growth in Seedlings
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: growth, regions of growth, apical meristem, root tip, primary growth, secondary growth, growth curve, measurement, maize, bean, seedling

slo.purpose: Learners use maize and bean seedlings to find where growth occurs in a plant, measure growth over time, and plot growth curves. This helps explain why maize and bean plants planted on the same day grow differently in height, stem thickness and root depth.
slo.knowledge: Growth is a permanent increase in size and dry mass. In seedlings, growth in length is concentrated in specific regions: root tips, shoot tips and, in maize, the base of the leaves. Growth can be measured as height, length, width or dry mass. A growth curve (sigmoid or S-shaped) plots growth against time and shows slow, rapid and slowing phases. This links to primary growth (apical meristems) and secondary growth (lateral meristems), which students sketched in earlier lessons.
slo.skills: Plan and carry out an investigation (marking seedlings with ink at equal intervals and measuring using a ruler or string); collect and record data in a table; analyse and interpret data by drawing a growth curve; construct explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; develop and revise models.
slo.attitudes: Unity: learners work harmoniously with peers when marking, measuring and recording data. Learning to Learn: learners reflect on their own work and adjust their measurements and explanations accordingly. Appreciation of accuracy, patience and honesty in recording data.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Raised for next lesson: How can we measure growth, and do plants have hormones that control it?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 5 showed that stems thicken and lengthen through primary and secondary growth, but it did not show WHERE growth happens on a living seedling or HOW it can be measured. Lesson 6 gives students quantitative evidence (measurements and growth curves) that growth is localised in particular regions and proceeds at different rates over time. This helps explain why the maize and bean seedlings in the farmer's field differ in height, root depth and branching. The question raised for Lesson 7 is: Do we have hormones in plants?
slo.safetyNotes: Use washable or non-toxic ink or a pencil/thread for marking; do not use permanent markers on soft root tips. Handle seedlings gently. Wash hands after handling soil and seedlings. Dispose of seedlings and soil in the school compost or garden. Keep razor blades away from learners; the teacher alone cuts any material. Sit and move calmly around crowded benches. Use readings from the textbook (or printed page) if no seedlings are available.

LESSONS.overview: Students return to the farmer's field: the maize and bean seeds were planted on the same day, yet the seedlings grow at different rates and in different parts. Learners predict where on a seedling growth happens, then mark young maize and bean seedling roots and shoots with equally spaced ink lines (every 5 mm or 1 cm) and observe or use prepared class data on how the marks spread apart. In groups of 4-5 they measure, tabulate and plot seedling height against time to produce a growth curve, then use the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning strategy to explain where and how growth occurs. The Driving Question Board (DQB) is updated with the new question 'Do we have hormones in plants?' and learners revise their models of maize and bean growth. The lesson relies on local materials (germinated maize and beans, ink, thread, rulers, graph paper) and needs no electricity or internet.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the farmer's field where maize and beans were planted together after the rains and show different growth. Individually they draw a seedling of maize and of bean in their notebooks and predict: (a) Where on the seedling does growth in length take place: all along the root and shoot, or only in certain regions? (b) Will a bean seedling and a maize seedling grow at the same speed each day? They sketch a quick prediction graph of 'height against time' for 30 days. They then discuss with a partner and share with the class using Think-Pair-Share.
framework.teacherMoves: Display on the board a sketch of the farmer's field with maize and bean seedlings. Say: 'The farmer in Nakuru planted maize and beans on the same day. Look at your drawings from Lesson 5. Where do you think the plant gets longer?' Give 1 minute of silent individual THINK time. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking the question before taking any answer. Then pair learners (2 minutes). Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) to share, and ask: 'What makes you think that?' Record 2-3 competing predictions on the board without judging them (e.g. 'whole root grows' vs 'only the tip grows'). Clarify the words 'region' and 'growth curve' in simple English. Ask learners to hold up fingers (1-5) showing how confident they are.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) combined with Think-Pair-Share. Making an explicit prediction exposes prior ideas (e.g. that the whole root elongates evenly) so that the evidence in the Observe phase can confirm or challenge them. Think-Pair-Share gives every learner time to formulate and rehearse an idea before speaking, including quieter learners in large classes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe and note on a checklist: Do learners draw a prediction showing a specific region of growth? Do they give a reason using Lesson 5 ideas such as 'dividing cells at the tip'? Listen for misconceptions such as 'plants grow from the base like hair' or 'growth is the same speed every day'. Count how many pairs can give a reason, not just an answer. Record the prediction on the board to return to in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4-5, learners work with germinated maize and bean seedlings (roots 2-3 cm long, prepared by the teacher or learners from earlier lessons and grown in wet cloth, newspaper or sawdust). Step 1: Gently mark the root of each seedling with thin ink (or tie fine thread) at equal intervals of 5 mm from the tip (about 5-6 marks). Step 2: Mark the shoot (plumule/epicotyl or the stem of the bean seedling) at 1 cm intervals from the top. Step 3: Return seedlings to the moist growing medium (a plastic bag, tin or cut jerrycan with soil) and re-measure after 24 and 48 hours. Step 4: Measure the distance between the marks and record in a table. Step 5: Using a second set of seedlings grown for 4 weeks (or class data supplied by the teacher), measure plant height every 3-4 days (day 0, 3, 7, 10, 14, 21, 28) for maize and bean and record in a table. Step 6: Plot a growth curve (height against time) on graph paper. Where seedlings are not available, learners use the data table below from a teacher-prepared handout (maize height in cm: day 0 = 1, day 7 = 4, day 14 = 14, day 21 = 32, day 28 = 48, day 35 = 55; bean: day 0 = 1, day 7 = 3, day 14 = 9, day 21 = 18, day 28 = 24, day 35 = 26) and plot both curves on the same axes. Learners note which marks moved furthest apart (root tip region) and which stayed together (older region).
framework.teacherMoves: Before class: prepare seedlings in advance by soaking maize and bean seeds (Kenya hybrid maize such as H614 and common beans such as Rosecoco or Mwitemania) and germinating them in damp cloth for 3-4 days. Prepare one set of seedlings per group (3 maize, 3 bean), a ruler, thread, washable ink or pencil, and graph paper. Demonstrate the marking on one seedling (touch gently and mark lightly, do not press). Circulate and ask: 'Which marks have moved apart the most? What does that tell you about where cells are dividing and growing?' and 'Why do we mark at equal distances?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call at least 5 different groups to report their measurements from different regions. Prompt: 'How did the root tip differ from the older part of the root?' Ask groups to check each other's readings for accuracy (parallax, starting at zero). If connectivity is available, show the germination time-lapse video; if not, use the teacher-prepared photo set or board drawings. Remind groups of roles: marker, measurer, recorder, reporter (Unity).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe step) with data tables and growth curves. Marking equal intervals makes growth visible and measurable, so learners see that growth is localised (apical regions) rather than uniform. Plotting the curve moves them from raw numbers to a pattern (slow start, rapid middle phase, levelling off), which is the pattern behind the farmer's different-sized plants.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist during the practical: Marks made at equal intervals (Y/N); measurements recorded to the nearest mm; table complete with units; roles shared among members; seedlings handled gently. Check graphs for correct axes (time on x-axis, height on y-axis), labelled units, a smooth curve of best fit, and the three phases identified. Oral probes: 'Which interval had the fastest growth? How do you know from your graph?' Note misconceptions such as joining points with a ruler as straight lines, or claiming bean and maize curves are identical.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups return to their predictions and use the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) strategy to explain where growth occurs and how it changes over time. Claim: 'Growth in length is concentrated at the root tip and shoot tip (apical meristems), and the rate of growth changes over time.' Evidence: they cite their own data (e.g. marks nearest the root tip moved furthest apart; maize height rose from 4 cm to 32 cm between days 7 and 21 while beans rose from 3 to 18 cm). Reasoning: they link this to cell division in meristems and cell elongation behind the tip (primary growth), to the later thickening of stems by the vascular cambium (secondary growth from Lesson 5), and to the S-shaped growth curve: slow phase (lag, seed uses stored food), rapid phase (log, active division and photosynthesis), and slowing phase (stationary, limited resources and maturity). They compare maize (monocot, fibrous roots, no secondary growth) and bean (dicot, taproot, can thicken) and suggest why the two curves differ. They then use Think-Pair-Share to compare their CER statement with another group's.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the CER frame: 'I claim that ___. My evidence is ___. This is because ___.' Model one sentence with a different example, e.g. 'Kenyan bamboo and sugarcane in Kisumu grow very fast at the nodes.' Ask: 'Using your data, where does growth in length happen?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 groups. Press for reasoning: 'Why do the marks near the tip move apart but those higher up do not?' Introduce key terms with simple definitions on the board: meristem (region of dividing cells), elongation, primary growth (growth in length), secondary growth (growth in girth), growth curve. Ask: 'What would happen to the maize seedling if a goat nibbled the tip?' to test understanding. Link back to the phenomenon: 'How does this help explain why some farmer's plants were taller than others after two weeks?' Address misconceptions: growth is not the same as development; growth is not only height. Leave the question open: 'But what controls the cells at the tip to divide and elongate?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Think-Pair-Share. CER requires learners to support a claim with their own measured data and connect it to biological ideas (meristems, primary and secondary growth), which moves them from describing to explaining. Comparing statements with another group exposes gaps in reasoning and builds scientific argumentation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a CER rubric: Claim is clear and specific (region named); Evidence includes at least two numerical values from the data; Reasoning links to meristems or cell division/elongation and to the three phases of the growth curve. Look for learners who use the terms 'apical meristem' and 'growth curve' correctly. Oral probing: 'What does the steep part of the curve show?' Peer review: each group exchanges CER statements and gives one 'star' (strength) and one 'step' (improvement). Note groups needing support with reasoning for re-teaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners go to the class Driving Question Board (a chart or a wall section) and revisit the main question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' Each group writes on sticky notes (or paper strips): (1) what they learned today that helps answer a DQB question (e.g. 'Growth is concentrated at the tips, and a growth curve shows different rates over time'), and (2) one new question (e.g. 'Do we have hormones in plants?', 'What makes the cells at the tip divide?', 'Why does a maize stalk grow taller than a bean vine?'). They place answered questions in the 'We are beginning to answer' area and new questions in the 'New questions' area. They also complete an exit ticket individually.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which questions did we answer a little more today?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to place a note and justify it with evidence from their data. Guide them to the question that links to the next lesson: 'We saw that the tip grows. What do you think tells the tip to grow? Is something inside the plant sending a signal?' Highlight the question 'Do we have hormones in plants?' and circle it as the focus of Lesson 7. Hand out exit tickets: 'What evidence did we gather today? How does this help answer our driving question?' Collect for review. If the class is large, have group representatives post notes while others write exit tickets.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning using the Driving Question Board. The DQB links each lesson to the anchoring phenomenon, helps learners see their progress, and turns gaps in understanding into the next question, creating a coherent storyline from measurement to hormones.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket (collect and review): indicators of success are (a) names at least one piece of evidence (e.g. 'marks near the root tip moved apart 8 mm') and (b) links it to the driving question (e.g. 'different parts and stages of growth help explain why the plants differ'). Check that the new question posted is productive (e.g. about what controls growth). Sort tickets into three piles (secure, partly secure, needs help) to plan Lesson 7 groupings.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit their Day 1 drawing and explanation of how maize and bean plants grow and revise their models. Each group updates a poster-size model (on manila paper) showing: a maize and a bean seedling with labelled regions of primary growth (apical meristems at root tip and shoot tip, region of elongation) and secondary growth (vascular cambium thickening in the bean stem); a small growth curve with the three phases labelled; and arrows showing factors (water, oxygen, temperature, stored food, light) that influence growth. They add a 'What is still missing?' box with a question mark for what controls the tip (to be explored in Lesson 7). Groups then do a short Gallery Walk: they display models, move to another group's poster, and leave one comment using 'I like... I wonder... A suggestion...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out Day 1 drawings from the learner folders. Say: 'Compare your first idea with what you know now. What would you change and why?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Provide model criteria on the board: labelled regions of growth; growth curve with phases; link to the farmer's maize and beans; evidence used. During the Gallery Walk (6-8 minutes), rotate groups every 2 minutes and cold-call 3 groups to share the best suggestion received and how they will use it. Ask: 'What can your model explain now that it could not explain on Day 1? What can it not yet explain?' Reinforce the need for an explanation of control (hormones). Display models in the class for use in later lessons. Remind learners that the tree nursery project later in the unit will need them to understand where roots and shoots grow on cuttings.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision plus Gallery Walk with peer review. Revising the Day 1 model with new evidence shows learners how their thinking has changed, and peer comments strengthen explanations. Leaving a 'missing piece' in the model (what controls growth) builds motivation for Lesson 7 on plant hormones.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check using a rubric: regions of growth correctly labelled (apical meristems, elongation zone); distinguishes primary from secondary growth; growth curve included with three phases; link to maize and bean differences; evidence cited; at least one peer comment received and acted upon. Observe whether learners add accurate improvements, not just decoration. Quick quiz (3 questions) if time allows: (1) Name the region where root growth is greatest. (2) What is shown by the steep part of an S-shaped curve? (3) Which plant, maize or bean, undergoes secondary growth? Record those who need further support.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did all groups mark and measure accurately, and did the data show clear localised growth? Which learners could write a full CER statement with numerical evidence, and who relied only on description? Were there misconceptions (e.g. whole root grows evenly, growth equals height only, growth curve is a straight line)? Did sharing of rulers and seedlings work in a large class, and would pre-marked seedlings or the teacher-prepared data table have helped? Was WAIT TIME used consistently and did cold-calling include quieter learners? Did the DQB question 'Do we have hormones in plants?' arise from learners themselves? Plan adjustments for Lesson 7 using the exit tickets, for example by grouping learners who need support with growth curves.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We marked maize and bean seedlings at equal intervals and measured how the marks moved apart over time. We also measured seedling height at intervals and plotted a growth curve. The marks near the root tip and shoot tip moved apart the most, and the curve showed a slow start, a rapid middle phase, and a levelling-off phase.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Growth in length is concentrated in specific regions (apical meristems at the root and shoot tips, followed by elongation), while stems thicken through secondary growth in some plants such as beans. Growth can be measured and shown on a growth curve that is S-shaped. Maize and bean seedlings grow at different rates and in different ways.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The maize and bean plants planted on the same day differ in height, root depth and branching because growth occurs in particular regions and at different rates in each plant type and over time. The sigmoid growth curve and the types of growth (primary and secondary) help explain these differences. What controls the cells at the tips to divide and elongate is still unknown, which raises the next question: Do we have hormones in plants?

LESSONS.title: Plant Hormones: What Controls Growth in Maize and Bean Seedlings?
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: plant hormones, auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, ethylene, apical dominance, germination, dormancy, secondary growth, regions of growth

slo.purpose: Learners use a video and a reading on plant hormones to work out how chemical messengers coordinate germination, shoot and root growth, branching and dormancy. They then apply this to explain why maize and bean seedlings planted on the same day with the same rain grow differently. The lesson also links back to the primary and secondary growth modelled earlier and leads to the question: how can we measure growth?
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to demonstrate the role of hormones in plant growth and development: auxins (cell elongation, apical dominance, rooting of cuttings), gibberellins (breaking dormancy, stem elongation, germination), cytokinins (cell division, lateral bud growth), abscisic acid (dormancy, closing stomata) and ethylene (fruit ripening).
slo.skills: Developing and using models; analysing and interpreting data; constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; obtaining, evaluating and communicating information from a video and a reading; asking questions.
slo.attitudes: Unity: works harmoniously with others while discussing evidence in groups. Learning to Learn: reflects on own work and adjusts it as new evidence appears. Appreciation of the importance of growth and development in plants (SLO h). Financial Literacy and Prevention of Global Warming: links hormones to tree nursery cuttings and seedling sales.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-6 covered seed structure, dormancy, germination conditions and types, and primary and secondary growth. This lesson adds the chemical control behind those processes: why seeds that look healthy differ in germination time, and why stems elongate, roots deepen and branches form. It creates a need to measure growth (the question raised for Lesson 8) and connects to the tree nursery project, where natural hormone sources such as bulb onions, Aloe and cinnamon help roots form on cuttings.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous chemicals are used. If learners handle seedlings or soil, they should wash hands afterwards. Do not taste any plant material or seeds, as some bean seeds are treated with pesticide. Keep walkways clear during the Gallery Walk. Natural rooting materials (onion, Aloe, cinnamon) are for external use only, and anyone with skin allergies should avoid them.

LESSONS.overview: The lesson opens with the anchoring phenomenon: maize and beans planted together after rain behave differently. Learners predict what invisible internal factor could explain this. They watch the Khan Academy video on major plant hormones (or hear the teacher-prepared narration if there is no connectivity) and read the accompanying notes on hormone roles. They record evidence in a hormone table and use Think-Pair-Share and CER to explain parts of the phenomenon. The Driving Question Board (DQB) is updated, and learners revise their Day 1 model by adding hormones as the control system. The lesson ends with an exit ticket and the new question: how can we measure growth?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the phenomenon sketch on the board (time-lapse stills or a teacher drawing): maize and bean seeds planted the same day in a shamba in Molo after rain. Some seedlings are tall, some are short, one bean has side branches and one seed has not germinated. On a half-page they individually write a prediction for 'What inside the plant could be controlling when a seed germinates, how tall the shoot grows and whether branches form?' and draw a quick arrow diagram. They then share with a partner (Think-Pair-Share) and add one idea from the partner in a different colour.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the sketch and say: 'Same day, same rain, same shamba. Why do these plants behave differently?' Give 10-15 seconds of silent WAIT TIME before anyone speaks. Say: 'Write one idea. Think about what messages a plant might use, since it has no brain or nerves.' Allow 3 minutes for writing, then 3 minutes for pairs. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) with: 'Tell us your partner's idea, not your own.' Record words such as 'chemical', 'food store' and 'water' on the board without judging. Circle any learner idea about 'chemical messengers' and say: 'Keep that word in mind; we will test it today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share, within Predict-Observe-Explain (POE). Individual thinking lets every learner commit to an idea before the video. Pair talk makes learners voice and refine reasoning. Saying a partner's idea builds listening and unity. Recorded predictions give a baseline to compare with video evidence later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: (1) each learner writes a prediction and a diagram within 3 minutes; (2) at least 3 of 4 cold-called learners accurately restate their partner's idea; (3) count learners who mention a chemical or internal signal rather than only external factors such as water or soil. Oral probe: 'What makes you think that?' Note misconceptions such as 'plants grow only because of rain' or 'plants cannot send signals'.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4-5 (sharing one textbook or reading per group), learners watch the Khan Academy video 'Major plant hormones (& how to remember) | Control & Coordination | class 10 | Biology' (or hear the teacher's narrated version with chalkboard drawings if there is no electricity or internet). Each group fills in a hormone evidence table with columns: Hormone | Where made | What it does | Link to maize/bean phenomenon. Roles within the group: Reader, Recorder, Reporter, Materials/Time keeper. After the video, groups read the notes on the role of plant hormones and their functions and add details to the table. They highlight at least one example for each of: auxin (shoot elongation, apical dominance, rooting of cuttings), gibberellins (breaking dormancy, germination, stem elongation), cytokinins (cell division, lateral bud growth), abscisic acid (dormancy, stomatal closure) and ethylene (fruit ripening, e.g. bananas or mangoes sold in Mombasa).
framework.teacherMoves: Before the video say: 'Watch for one hormone that could explain a seed that is healthy but has not germinated, and one that could explain side branches.' Pause the video at each hormone and ask: 'What did you see or hear?' Give 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME, then cold-call 2 groups per pause. Offline fallback: read the narration aloud in short chunks and draw the hormone effects on the board (a tall maize shoot, a bean with side branches, a ripening banana). Clarify terms: 'elongation means getting longer', 'dormancy means a resting seed', 'lateral bud means a side bud'. Circulate and ask: 'Which part of the table helps explain the seed that did not germinate?' Remind groups to share books and to write in simple, clear scientific English. Link to the tree nursery project: 'Why might bulb onion or Aloe extract help cuttings form roots?' (natural rooting hormones such as auxins).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe step) with structured evidence recording. The table makes learners pull evidence from two sources (video and reading) and tie each hormone to a part of the phenomenon. Pausing the video for prediction and discussion keeps learners actively connecting new information to their earlier predictions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist during group work: (1) every group has at least 4 hormones recorded with correct location and function; (2) each learner fulfils a role; (3) the 'Link to phenomenon' column is filled with a specific link (e.g. 'gibberellins could break dormancy in the bean that has not germinated'). Oral probes: 'Which hormone makes stems longer?' and 'What does apical dominance mean?' Watch for the misconception that hormones are only found in animals or that one hormone does only one job.

framework.learnerExperience: Using the evidence table, groups write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) explanation for one part of the phenomenon assigned by the teacher: (A) a healthy bean seed that germinates late or not at all; (B) maize shoots that elongate quickly; (C) bean plants that develop side branches while maize stays unbranched; (D) farmers in Kericho or Nyeri rooting tea or tree cuttings with natural hormone sources. Each group writes: Claim (what hormone/process explains it), Evidence (from video, reading or earlier lessons such as seed dormancy and germination conditions), Reasoning (how the hormone causes the effect, linking to cell division, elongation or secondary growth). Groups then do a short Gallery Walk, reading other CERs and leaving one sticky note or pencil comment ('I agree because...' or 'What about...?').
framework.teacherMoves: Model one CER on the board, e.g. 'Claim: Auxin from the tip of the bean stem keeps side buds from growing. Evidence: the video showed that removing the tip allowed side shoots to grow. Reasoning: auxin moves down and suppresses lateral buds, so removing the tip lowers auxin and lets cytokinins promote branching.' Say: 'Your reasoning must say how, not just what.' Allow 8 minutes writing. Say: 'Stop and look at your evidence. Does it support your claim?' Give 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME. For the Gallery Walk, set 6 minutes and rotate groups every 2 minutes. Cold-call 3 groups to share one comment they received and how they will revise their explanation. Probe: 'Which factor besides hormones also affects germination, such as water, oxygen or temperature? How do they interact?' Clarify that hormones respond to environmental conditions and do not replace them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) plus Gallery Walk. CER forces learners to justify explanations with evidence and causal reasoning, and the Gallery Walk exposes them to different parts of the phenomenon and to peer critique, helping them build a connected explanation of why maize and beans differ.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a CER rubric (0-2 per part): the claim names a correct hormone or process; the evidence is drawn from the video, reading or earlier lessons; the reasoning explains the mechanism. Success indicator: at least 80% of groups reach a score of 4 or more out of 6. Peer review: each group gives one specific comment. Oral probes identify misconceptions such as 'hormones are food for the plant' or 'gibberellins cause dormancy'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class DQB (on manila paper or the chalkboard) holding the driving question, 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' In pairs they write on sticky notes or paper strips: (1) one thing they now understand about hormones and growth, and (2) one new question. They place them on the DQB under the headings 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New questions'. They add the new question 'How can you measure growth in plants?' and others such as 'Do maize and beans have the same amounts of hormones?', 'Can farmers use hormones to improve yields?' and 'How can we show growth on a graph?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. What can we now move from questions to answers?' Allow 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME. Invite 3 pairs (cold-called) to move a question and justify with evidence from today's video or reading. Say: 'Which new question do we need data to answer?' Guide learners to the point that to compare maize and bean growth, we need measurements, introducing Lesson 8. Tag questions by type (can investigate with seedlings, need reading, need video). If paper is scarce, use the chalkboard and one scribe per group.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the Driving Question Board. Moving questions across categories shows learners how evidence advances understanding. Generating new questions keeps them engaged in inquiry and links each lesson to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of pairs write one accurate statement using the term 'hormone' and one testable question. Observe whether learners justify the placement of a note with evidence. Look for questions that move from 'what' to 'how' or 'why'. Note any unresolved confusions to address in Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their Day 1 model/drawing of what causes differences in maize and bean germination and growth. Individually, in a different colour, they revise it to include: (a) hormones (gibberellins, auxins, cytokinins, abscisic acid) with arrows showing where they act on the seed, shoot, root and lateral buds; (b) links to earlier lessons (dormancy, germination conditions, primary growth at root and shoot tips, secondary growth in woody dicots, e.g. a mukau or jacaranda tree); and (c) a short caption explaining one cause of the differences in maize and beans. They swap with a partner for peer review using two stars and a wish.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your Day 1 model was your first guess. What would you add or change now, and what evidence made you change it?' Give 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME before they start. Circulate, and ask 5 learners: 'Where is the hormone made, and what does it do here?' Prompt: 'Show what happens when the shoot tip is cut.' Remind learners to label clearly. After peer review, cold-call 3 learners to share one revision and its evidence. Collect the models for a model check. Hand out exit tickets: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision. Learners compare earlier ideas with new evidence, which strengthens conceptual change and shows learning growth (Learning to Learn). Peer review gives feedback on clarity and accuracy.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check: look for at least three hormones with correct locations and functions, at least one link to dormancy or germination, and one link to branching or elongation. Peer review: two stars and a wish with specific wording. Exit ticket: success if the learner names one piece of evidence (e.g. 'the video showed that removing the shoot tip allowed side shoots to grow') and links it to the driving question. A quick quiz of 3 questions (name the hormone for dormancy-breaking, elongation, ripening) can be used for the last 3 minutes.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners connect hormone roles to the maize and bean phenomenon, or only list functions? (2) Which hormone ideas caused confusion (e.g. gibberellins vs auxins, or apical dominance)? (3) Did group roles work with shared textbooks and large classes? (4) Was the offline narration as effective as the video? (5) How did predictions at the start compare with final models? Use exit tickets to sort learners into those who need re-teaching on hormone functions, those ready for measuring growth in Lesson 8, and those who could extend to agricultural uses such as rooting powders in tree nurseries. Plan to bring maize and bean seedlings (or marked seedlings grown in tins) next lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We watched a video and read about the major plant hormones (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene) and recorded where each is made and what it does in the plant.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate germination, dormancy, shoot and root growth, branching and fruit ripening. They work together with environmental factors such as water, oxygen and temperature.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Differences in germination, emergence and growth between maize and bean plants can partly be explained by hormone balance: for example, gibberellins and abscisic acid affect dormancy and germination time, auxin affects shoot elongation and apical dominance, and cytokinins affect branching. To compare growth we now need to measure it.

LESSONS.title: Measuring Growth: Seedling Height, Stem Width and Growth Curves of Maize and Beans
LESSONS.duration: 80 minutes (double period), with daily 5-minute measurement checks beforehand
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: growth, measurement, growth curve, sigmoid curve, lag phase, exponential phase, stationary phase, seedling height, stem width, maize, beans, hormones

slo.purpose: Learners record seedling height and stem width data from maize and bean seedlings, plot growth curves, and use the curves to explain why the two crops, planted on the same day after the same rain, grow at different rates. The lesson ends with the new question: Do we have hormones in plants?
slo.knowledge: Growth is a permanent increase in size, dry mass or cell number. It can be measured as height, stem width, leaf area, fresh mass or dry mass. A typical growth curve is S-shaped (sigmoid), with a lag phase, a rapid (exponential) phase and a stationary phase. Maize (monocot, epigeal/hypogeal context from earlier lessons) and beans (dicot) have different growth patterns and rates.
slo.skills: Measuring with a ruler, string and thread. Recording data in a table. Plotting line graphs. Interpreting graph shapes. Making Claims with Evidence and Reasoning (CER). Working in groups and giving peer feedback. (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Engaging in Argument from Evidence.)
slo.attitudes: Unity: works harmoniously with group members while measuring and recording. Learning to Learn: reflects on own data and graphs and corrects errors. Appreciation of the importance of growth and development in plants. Curiosity about what controls growth.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? Sub-question for today: How can we measure growth, and what do growth curves tell us about why maize and beans grow differently?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-7 gave evidence on seed structure, dormancy, germination conditions and regions of growth. Lesson 8 turns observations into quantitative data. The curves show that growth is not constant: it speeds up and slows down, and maize and beans differ. This raises the question of what controls the timing and speed of growth, leading to Lesson 9 on plant hormones (Do we have hormones in plants?).
slo.safetyNotes: Handle seedlings gently and wash hands after touching soil. Use rulers and thread, not sharp blades. Keep walkways clear of tins and trays. Wash hands before leaving the class. No electricity or internet is needed; the time-lapse video is optional, and the teacher's chart is the alternative.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the farmer's puzzle: maize and beans planted on the same day after the same rain look different as they grow. Using seedlings grown in tins, cartons or sacks over earlier lessons (or teacher-prepared data sets for days missed), groups measure shoot height with a ruler and stem width with thread wrapped around the stem and measured against the ruler. They compile data for Days 0-21, plot growth curves on graph paper, compare the S-shaped curve of one crop against the other, and write CER explanations. A Gallery Walk lets groups review each other's graphs. The DQB gains the question 'Do we have hormones in plants?' and the class revises its model of growth.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the farmer's field with maize and beans. Teacher draws empty axes on the board (height in cm vs time in days). Individually, learners sketch on a half-page what they predict the height of a maize seedling and a bean seedling will look like over 21 days: a straight line, a curve that keeps rising, or something else. They also predict which will be taller at Day 7 and Day 21, and write one reason. They then pair up and compare, then share with the class (Think-Pair-Share).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Imagine you walk past the farmer's shamba every day for three weeks with a ruler. Sketch what the height of the maize and beans would look like on a graph. Do not talk yet.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then 2 minutes of silent sketching. Say: 'Turn to your partner. Show your sketch and explain why you drew it that way.' Circulate and listen for 'it grows the same amount every day'. Cold-call 4 pairs to describe their sketches; draw 2-3 different sketches on the board without judging them. Ask: 'Does anyone think the growth rate changes? Why?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with Think-Pair-Share. Predictions make learners commit to an idea about the shape of growth, such as a straight line, so the real data can challenge it. Pair talk lets every learner voice reasoning before the whole class hears it.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation indicators: learners draw a labelled axis with units; give a reason linked to the phenomenon (for example 'maize is a grass so it grows tall quickly'); at least 4 pairs share. Note the number of learners who predict a straight line, which is a misconception to revisit. Record the count on the checklist.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4-5 with roles (measurer, reader, recorder, checker), learners measure the height of 3 maize and 3 bean seedlings from the class nursery, from soil level to the shoot tip, in cm. They measure stem width by wrapping thread around the stem once, then measuring the thread length against a ruler and dividing by 3 (circumference / 3 ≈ diameter). They add today's readings to the group table from earlier days (Days 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21). Where seedlings were missed, the teacher gives a back-up data table (for example maize mean height: Day 3 = 2 cm, 6 = 8, 9 = 18, 12 = 32, 15 = 48, 18 = 58, 21 = 62; bean mean height: Day 3 = 1, 6 = 3, 9 = 7, 12 = 12, 15 = 17, 18 = 20, 21 = 21). Learners calculate mean values for each day, plot both height curves on graph paper using different colours, and plot stem width as a second graph if time permits. They note where the curve is flat, steep or levelling off.
framework.teacherMoves: Demonstrate once: 'Place the zero of the ruler at the soil surface, not at the pot edge. Read at eye level.' Say: 'Measure three seedlings per crop, then find the mean. Why do we use more than one seedling?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners. Circulate with the observation checklist. Prompt: 'Which part of your curve is steepest? Which days are slow?' If groups plot a straight line through points, ask: 'Do all your points lie on your line? What does the curve actually do?' Pre-print or draw a graph template on the board for groups with limited graph paper. Label the phases: lag, rapid, stationary. Without electricity, use a teacher-prepared chart in place of the time-lapse video; if power is available, show 2 minutes of the time-lapse after plotting.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data collection with Analyzing and Interpreting Data, and visual inference. Turning numbers into graphs lets learners see patterns of changing growth rates that are hidden in the table, building a quantitative picture of the farmer's puzzle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: ruler zero at soil level; reading at eye level; thread method used correctly; mean calculated correctly; axes labelled with units; points plotted accurately (within half a small square); roles shared fairly. Oral probe: 'Why is the bean curve lower than the maize curve at Day 15?' Note learners who confuse growth rate (slope) with total height.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups interpret their curves: they identify the lag phase (slow start while the seed absorbs water and mobilises food stores), the exponential phase (rapid cell division and elongation), and the stationary phase (growth slows as the plant reaches maturity or resources limit it). They write a CER statement: Claim (for example 'Maize grows faster than beans between Days 6 and 15'), Evidence (specific numbers from their table and graph), Reasoning (links to cotyledon food stores, shoot structure, leaf area for photosynthesis, and the monocot/dicot differences from Lessons 1-7). They also compare height with stem width: maize gains height quickly, while bean stems thicken differently. Pairs swap CER statements and give one star (strength) and one wish (improvement). A short whole-class discussion links to the farmer's puzzle and to the seeds that failed to germinate (no data, so no curve).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Point to the steepest part of the maize curve. What was happening in the seedling then?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups. Provide the CER frame on the board: 'I claim... The evidence is... This is because...'. Press for numbers: 'Which two values show that? Subtract them for me.' Clarify difficult terms: sigmoid means S-shaped; exponential means increasing faster and faster. Ask: 'Planted on the same day with the same rain, why do the curves still differ?' Accept ideas such as seed size, food reserves, genes, temperature, soil nutrients. Then ask: 'Something inside the plant seems to speed up and slow down growth at different times. What could be controlling that?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Do not give the answer; let it lead to the DQB.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with peer review. CER forces learners to tie each statement about growth to specific numbers and biological reasons instead of opinion, and star/wish feedback develops scientific argumentation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Rubric for CER (0-3): claim is testable; evidence cites at least two numbers from the graph; reasoning links to biology (food stores, cell division, leaf area). Indicator of mastery: learner correctly names the three phases on the curve. Quick oral quiz of 3 questions: 'What does the steep part of the curve show?' 'Why does the curve level off?' 'Which measurement tells us about thickening?' Note misconceptions such as 'a flat line means the plant has died'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB. In groups they write on sticky notes or paper: (1) one new piece of evidence from today (for example 'Maize shows a rapid growth phase between Days 6 and 15') and (2) one new question. They place these under the matching DQB categories (seed structure, dormancy, germination conditions, growth measurement). The class notices that many questions ask what controls the speed and timing of growth and agrees on the lesson's new question: 'Do we have hormones in plants?' Learners also move at least one earlier question to 'partly answered'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our Driving Question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants? What does today's graph add?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to post notes and read them aloud. Read the question aloud and say: 'Animals have hormones such as insulin and adrenaline. Do we have hormones in plants? What evidence would we need?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Write the question in a coloured marker at the top of the DQB for Lesson 9. Ask: 'Which earlier questions can we now partly answer?' and have learners tick them. If no wall space is available, use manila paper or a chalkboard section.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning using the Driving Question Board. Learners link today's data to the driving question and see their own questions shaping the next lesson, which builds ownership and coherence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: sticky notes include evidence rather than only opinions; new questions are testable; at least 5 groups contribute; learners move or tick at least one earlier question. Note whether learners can explain why the hormone question follows from the curves. Exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit their Day 1 drawings and explanations of why maize and beans grow differently. Individually, they add or revise parts of the model: growth curve sketches for maize and beans with the three phases labelled; arrows showing food stores (endosperm in maize, cotyledons in beans) feeding early growth; and a question mark labelled 'something controls the speed? (hormones?)'. Groups then take part in a Gallery Walk, posting their graphs and revised models; each learner visits two other groups, leaves one comment on a sticky note ('I agree because...' or 'Have you considered...'), and returns to improve their own model using the feedback. Early finishers add a note on how a farmer in Kericho or Kitale could use growth curves to decide when to top-dress maize or weed beans.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Day 1 drawing. Use a different colour pen to show what you now know.' WAIT TIME 10 seconds, then 5 minutes of silent revision. Set the Gallery Walk: 'You have 8 minutes. Visit two groups. Leave one comment that refers to evidence.' Circulate and ask: 'Where on your model is the evidence from today's graph?' Cold-call 3 learners to describe one change they made and why. Close with the exit ticket on paper or as an oral round of 5 learners. Assign homework: observe and record a plant at home (for example sukuma wiki or a tree seedling) and bring one question about what makes it bend toward light.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision with Gallery Walk and peer review. Updating the Day 1 model with measured evidence shows learners how their understanding has changed. Peer comments push them to justify the model with data, which prepares them to add hormones in Lesson 9.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check indicators: revised model includes the three growth phases; food store arrows; differences between maize and beans; and an unanswered question about control. Peer review comments cite evidence. Exit ticket sorting: 'Fully', 'Partly' or 'Not yet' for the target 'I can draw and interpret a growth curve'. Follow up with learners who place the stationary phase incorrectly.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which groups showed accurate measuring and plotting, and which struggled with scale or the thread method? Did learners move beyond 'maize is taller' to explain the change in growth rate using phases of the curve? How many learners still predicted straight-line growth after the data? Which Kenyan contexts (the farmer's shamba, tins of maize and beans, top-dressing in Kitale or Kericho) helped learners connect to the phenomenon? Was there enough time for the Gallery Walk without electricity or full graph paper? What adjustments are needed for large classes (for example, one measurement station per group and shared rulers)? Which learners need support with terminology (sigmoid, exponential, stationary) before Lesson 9 on plant hormones?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We measured the height and stem width of maize and bean seedlings over time and plotted growth curves. Both curves were S-shaped, with a slow start, a rapid growth phase and a levelling-off phase, but maize grew faster and taller than beans in the same period.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Growth can be measured as height, stem width, mass or leaf area. A growth curve shows that growth rate changes over time (lag, exponential and stationary phases). Maize and beans differ in growth rate and pattern even when planted on the same day.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The growth rate changes because of food stores, cell division and elongation, leaf area for photosynthesis and the type of plant. Something inside the plant may be controlling the timing and speed of growth, so we ask: Do we have hormones in plants?
