LESSONS.title: Role of Hormones in Plant Growth and Development: Why Do Maize and Bean Plants Grow Differently?
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, ethylene, apical dominance, dormancy, germination, rooting hormone, pruning, tea plucking in Kericho, tree nursery

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how plant hormones coordinate germination, shoot and root growth, and branching, and use this evidence to explain why maize and bean plants planted on the same day after the same rain differ in germination, emergence and growth.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: demonstrate the role of hormones in plant growth and development (Specific Learning Outcome g); name the major plant hormones (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, ethylene) and state one function of each; explain apical dominance and how removing the shoot tip affects branching; relate hormone action to agriculture, e.g. pruning of tea in Kericho, rooting of cuttings, ripening of mangoes and bananas.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (hormone flow diagram); analysing and interpreting data from a video and a reading; constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; obtaining, evaluating and communicating information; recording data and drawing conclusions from a simple pruning demonstration.
slo.attitudes: Unity: works harmoniously with peers when analysing evidence and building a shared model. Learning to Learn: reflects on and revises own Day 1 ideas. Citizenship and Patriotism: values sharing seedlings and farming knowledge with the community. Financial Literacy: appreciates how hormone knowledge (pruning, rooting cuttings) can raise farm and nursery income. Prevention of Global Warming: appreciates tree nurseries as a way to mitigate climate change.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Lesson focus: What chemical messages inside the plant control when seeds germinate and how seedlings grow and branch?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-8 gathered evidence on seed structure, dormancy, germination conditions and types, primary and secondary growth, and growth curves. Learners now have a gap: the structures and conditions alone do not explain why seeds under identical rain behave differently or why some plants branch while others stay single-stemmed. Lesson 9 supplies the internal control mechanism, hormones, and sets up Lesson 10, the final revision of the class model and the claim on the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: Pruning demonstration: use clean, sharp scissors or a razor blade handled only by the teacher or one trained learner per group; cut away from the body. Do not taste any plant materials (onion, Aloe, cinnamon, bean seedlings) used in the demonstration. Wash hands after handling soil and plants. Keep seedling trays away from walkways. If any learner is allergic to Aloe sap or onion, they act as recorder only. Do not consume treated seeds or any seedlings from the experiment.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting what would happen if the tip of a young bean seedling were cut off, using a Think-Pair-Share. They then gather evidence from a time-lapse or teacher-prepared picture sequence (offline alternative: large chart drawings) showing hormone effects, and read a short passage on auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene, including apical dominance. A pruned versus unpruned bean seedling demonstration (set up earlier or shown live) supports the evidence. In the Explain phase learners write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement on how hormones help explain differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and beans, and connect it to Kenyan agriculture (tea plucking in Kericho, rooting cuttings with onion or Aloe in a school tree nursery, ripening bananas in Mombasa markets). They add questions and answers to the Driving Question Board and revise their Day 1 model by adding hormone arrows and labels. The lesson uses small groups, shared textbooks and locally available materials, and does not depend on electricity or the internet.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the farmer's maize and bean field after rainfall. The teacher shows a bean seedling in a cup (or a labelled drawing on the board) and asks: 'If a farmer pinches off the very top of this young bean plant, what will happen to the stems over the next two weeks?' Learners think silently for 1 minute and write a prediction and a reason in their notebooks. They pair up, compare predictions, then share. They also predict: 'What might be moving inside the plant that tells the seed when to germinate and the shoot when to grow?' Predictions are recorded on a class chart titled 'What we think controls plant growth'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember our farmer's field. Same rain, same day, but different results. Today we ask what is happening inside the plant.' Hold up the seedling and say: 'Write your prediction in one sentence and give a reason beginning with "because".' Give 60 seconds of silent think time. Then say: 'Turn to your partner and compare.' Circulate for 2 minutes and listen for ideas such as 'the plant will grow sideways' or 'the plant will die'. Ask: 'What do you think is sending signals in the plant?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups, including at least 2 who have not spoken yet, and record each prediction without judging it. Ask one follow-up: 'Who can tell us why they chose that?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share and Predict-Observe-Explain (POE): Individual thinking surfaces each learner's own ideas before any instruction, pairing lets learners rehearse and refine their reasoning in a low-risk setting, and public sharing creates a class record of predictions to test against evidence later. The prediction is directly linked to the phenomenon of different growth patterns in the same field.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation: Tick on a checklist how many learners write a prediction with a reason (target: at least 80%). Look for the misconception that plants grow only because of water and soil, with no internal control. Note learners who use words such as 'signal', 'chemical' or 'tip'. Oral probe: 'What makes you think the tip matters?' Learners who cannot give a reason are flagged for support during the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 5-6, learners gather evidence from three sources. (1) Video or picture sequence: they watch a short time-lapse of seedlings responding to hormones (if available; offline alternative: the teacher shows a prepared chart of four drawings: a seedling with intact tip, a seedling with the tip removed, a tip with an agar or soil block placed back on it, and a seedling bent toward light), and complete an observation table of what changed and where. (2) Reading: each group receives one section of the 'Plant Hormones' reading card (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene, plus apical dominance), and records the function and a Kenyan example in a table. Examples on the cards: tea pruning and plucking in Kericho to make bushes branch, bean and maize seed germination boosted by gibberellins, rooting of cuttings with natural sources of hormones such as bulb onion, Aloe and cinnamon in a school tree nursery, and ethylene ripening bananas and mangoes bought at Mombasa markets, and abscisic acid keeping dormant seeds from germinating in the dry season. (3) Pruning demonstration: the teacher shows two bean seedlings set up two weeks earlier, one with its tip pinched off and one intact, and learners measure height and count side branches, recording in a table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are now scientists collecting evidence. Write only what you can see, not what you think.' Before the video or chart, say: 'Watch for three things: where the change happens, what part of the plant responds, and how long it takes.' Play the video twice if available; if there is no electricity or internet, say: 'Our video is on paper today. Look closely at each drawing.' and walk the chart through step by step. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What is different between the seedling with the tip and the one without?' Cold-call 3 groups to report one observation each. Distribute reading cards (one per group, shared between 5-6 learners) and say: 'Read together. Underline the function of your hormone and one Kenyan example.' Clarify difficult terms on the board: 'hormone = chemical messenger', 'apical = at the top', 'dominance = control'. For the demonstration say: 'Compare the two plants. Count the side branches and measure the height with a ruler.' Safety: only the teacher handles the blade. Ask: 'Which plant is taller? Which is bushier? What might explain it?' Cold-call 4 learners for measurements, and record on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE), Observe step: learners test their earlier predictions against three independent sources of evidence (video or chart, text and a live demonstration). Triangulating sources helps them see that the same pattern appears repeatedly, which strengthens their later claims. Jigsaw-style sharing of reading cards also spreads the reading load, which suits large classes with limited textbooks.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: tick learners who (a) record observations without interpreting, (b) measure height correctly in cm, (c) count side branches accurately, and (d) take a role in the group. Success indicators: the observation table shows that the pruned seedling has more side branches and the intact seedling is taller; each group's reading table has the correct function for its hormone (e.g. auxin: cell elongation and apical dominance; gibberellins: seed germination and stem elongation; cytokinins: cell division and side-bud growth; abscisic acid: dormancy and closing stomata; ethylene: fruit ripening). Oral probes: 'Which hormone did you read about and what does it do?' Misconception to catch: 'Hormones are only found in animals.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners build a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement in their groups to answer: 'How do hormones help explain why maize and bean plants grown together differ in germination, emergence and growth?' They write the claim (e.g. 'Hormones such as gibberellins, abscisic acid and auxins control when seeds germinate and how the shoot and branches grow, so differences in hormone balance and response can cause different germination and growth'), then list at least two pieces of evidence (the pruned versus intact bean seedling data, the video or chart observations, the reading on abscisic acid and gibberellins in dormancy, and earlier lessons on dormancy and germination) and finally write the reasoning linking evidence to claim (e.g. 'When the tip, the source of auxin, was removed, side buds were released, showing that auxin from the tip suppresses side branches; this is apical dominance. Because maize is a monocot with one main stem and beans are dicots that can branch, their hormone responses and growth forms differ.'). Groups also explain farm applications: why tea farmers in Kericho prune bushes, why a nursery manager may dip cuttings in onion or Aloe extract, and why Mombasa traders put bananas in a closed sack to ripen them faster. Each group swaps its CER with another group for peer review using a three-point checklist: Is the claim clear? Is the evidence from our data? Does the reasoning link both?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A good scientific explanation has three parts: a claim, evidence and reasoning. Let us build one together.' Model one example on the board with a different question (e.g. 'Why do tea bushes in Kericho become bushy after pruning?'). Then say: 'Now do it for the maize and bean question.' Circulate and ask: 'What is your evidence for that?' and 'How does that evidence support your claim?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before offering any help. Cold-call 3 groups to read their claims and 3 different learners to give a piece of evidence. Ask the class: 'Do hormones act alone, or do they work together? Think about abscisic acid and gibberellins in seeds.' Take 2 more responses. Probe misconceptions: 'Does cutting the tip kill the plant? What did our data show?' Provide an extension challenge to faster groups: 'How could a farmer use this knowledge to get more branches on bean plants or more roots on a cutting?' Close by saying: 'Hormones are one part of the answer; the other parts are the seed structure, dormancy, water, oxygen and temperature from our earlier lessons.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with peer review: learners must justify claims with data they collected and explicitly connect the data to a scientific idea (apical dominance and hormonal control). Modelling the structure first reduces cognitive load and supports learners writing in a second language, while peer review teaches them to critique evidence, not opinions. Connecting to agriculture shows that the explanation has real-world value in Kenyan farming and tree nurseries.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review checklist and teacher scoring rubric (0-3) for each CER: claim present and answers the question; at least two pieces of evidence taken from data or reading; reasoning links evidence to hormone action. Success indicators: learners use terms such as 'auxin', 'apical dominance', 'gibberellin' and 'abscisic acid' correctly; evidence cites actual numbers (e.g. '4 side branches versus 0'). Oral probing identifies misconceptions: (a) 'hormones are the only factor in germination', (b) 'removing the tip kills the plant', (c) 'one hormone does one job only'. Quick quiz (3 questions, 3 minutes): name the hormone that breaks dormancy; state what apical dominance means; give one agricultural use of ethylene or pruning. Aim for 70% correct.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the main question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' Each group writes (a) one new answer or piece of evidence from today on a green sticky note or paper strip, e.g. 'Gibberellins and abscisic acid control dormancy and germination' or 'Auxin from the tip causes apical dominance', and (b) one new question on a different colour, e.g. 'How do hormones interact with water and temperature?' or 'Can we use onion or Aloe to root cuttings for our school nursery?'. Learners match their notes to earlier questions on the board and move any questions that have now been answered into the 'Answered' column. Learners also complete an exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let us see how today's evidence helps our big question. Each group, one answer and one new question.' Allow 3 minutes for writing. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which of our earlier questions can we now move to Answered?' Cold-call 3 groups to place a note and explain the link in one sentence. Ask: 'Which questions are still not answered?' and highlight 2 for Lesson 10 (e.g. 'How do all the factors work together?'). Link to the project: 'Our nursery project will use natural hormone sources such as onion, Aloe and cinnamon on stem cuttings. What would you test?' Collect exit tickets at the door.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the Driving Question Board: sorting and connecting questions shows learners the unit as a coherent story. Writing new questions encourages curiosity and gives the teacher information to shape Lesson 10. The exit ticket provides individual accountability for explaining how evidence connects to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket scoring: 2 points if the learner names specific evidence (e.g. 'the bean with its tip removed had more branches') and links it to the driving question; 1 point if only one part; 0 if blank or vague. Look for new questions that show deeper thinking (interaction of factors, applications). Observation: note groups where every member contributes to the notes. Oral probe: 'Which earlier lesson connects to today's hormone idea?' Use results to identify learners needing a short re-teach at the start of Lesson 10.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Day 1 drawings and explanations of why the maize and bean seeds behave differently. Individually, they revise the model by adding: (a) hormone labels and arrows (gibberellins promoting germination and stem elongation, abscisic acid maintaining dormancy, auxin from the shoot tip suppressing side buds, cytokinins promoting side bud growth and cell division); (b) a note on how hormones interact with water, oxygen, temperature, seed structure and dormancy from previous lessons; and (c) a short sentence beginning 'I changed my model because...'. They then take part in a Gallery Walk: groups display their revised models with seed structure drawings, germination results, growth curves and CER explanations. Learners walk around in rotation with sticky notes, leaving one 'star' (a strength) and one 'wish' (a suggestion) at each display. Finally, learners return to their own work and make one further improvement based on peer feedback.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your Day 1 model. What was missing? Add the hormones we learned about today and show how they connect to the other factors.' Give 10 minutes of individual work. Circulate and ask: 'Where on your model does the signal start? What does it do?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before responding to learners who hesitate. Then organise the Gallery Walk: 'Move clockwise every 2 minutes. Leave one star and one wish.' Cold-call 4 learners afterwards: 'What feedback helped you improve your model?' and 'What change did you make because of it?' Highlight strong models, particularly those linking hormones to both germination and growth, and say: 'Next lesson we will bring everything together into one final explanation and test our claim against all the evidence.' Remind learners to bring seedlings or notes from the nursery project.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision with Gallery Walk and peer review: revisiting Day 1 models and explicitly stating what changed helps learners see their own learning (metacognition, Learning to Learn). Peer feedback through stars and wishes builds Unity and develops the habit of critiquing ideas using evidence. Integrating hormones with previously studied factors guides learners toward a systems view of plant growth.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check indicators: the revised model includes at least three correctly labelled hormones with functions; arrows show the direction of cause and effect (e.g. tip, then auxin, then side buds suppressed); at least two earlier factors (water, oxygen, temperature, dormancy, seed structure) appear connected to hormones; the learner writes a clear 'I changed my model because...' statement. Peer review: star and wish notes are specific (e.g. 'Your arrow from the tip is clear' or 'Add where gibberellins act'). Teacher uses the observation checklist to record participation and feedback quality. Misconception check: models that show hormones acting alone, with no role for water or temperature, are flagged for discussion at the start of Lesson 10.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners connect hormones to the phenomenon of different germination and growth in maize and beans, or did they treat hormones as an isolated topic? (2) Which hormones were hardest for learners, and what examples (tea in Kericho, bananas in Mombasa, cuttings in a school nursery) helped most? (3) Were the pruning data clear enough to support CER claims, and would a longer observation time or a second demonstration have improved it? (4) Did cold-calling and wait time bring quieter learners into the discussion? (5) Were group sizes and shared reading cards manageable, and how did the offline alternatives work with no electricity? (6) Which misconceptions remain (hormones act alone; cutting the tip kills the plant; hormones exist only in animals), and how will they be addressed in Lesson 10? (7) Which questions on the Driving Question Board should shape the final synthesis? Record learner questions about the tree nursery project for follow-up.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a bean seedling with its tip removed grew more side branches but was shorter, while the intact seedling grew taller with few branches. We also saw (in the video or chart) how plant parts respond to hormones, e.g. bending toward light and rooting of cuttings, and we read that gibberellins, abscisic acid, cytokinins, auxins and ethylene each control different parts of growth.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that hormones are chemical messengers that control germination, dormancy, cell elongation, branching, rooting and fruit ripening. Auxin from the shoot tip causes apical dominance, and removing the tip releases side buds. Farmers use this knowledge when pruning tea in Kericho, rooting cuttings in tree nurseries and ripening bananas and mangoes.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Hormones help explain why maize and beans planted together on the same day can germinate, emerge and grow differently: the balance of gibberellins and abscisic acid affects whether a seed breaks dormancy, and auxin and cytokinins control shoot growth and branching, with differences in species and seed condition changing the outcome. These internal signals work together with water, oxygen, temperature and seed structure to produce the differences we saw in the farmer's field.

LESSONS.title: Synthesis and Application: Explaining the Farmer's Maize and Beans and Planning the Tree Nursery
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: final explanation, claim-evidence-reasoning, cumulative model, Driving Question Board, germination, dormancy, hypogeal, epigeal, primary growth, secondary growth, auxin, apical dominance, stem cuttings, tree nursery

slo.purpose: Learners synthesise evidence from Lessons 1-9 to write a final Claim-Evidence-Reasoning explanation of why maize and bean seeds planted on the same day after rain differ in germination, emergence and growth. They complete and compare their final model with the Day 1 model, close out the Driving Question Board, and apply their learning to plan a tree nursery using stem cuttings and natural rooting hormones (bulb onion, Aloe, cinnamon).
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) explain how seed structure (monocot maize vs dicot bean), dormancy, germination conditions (water, oxygen, suitable temperature), type of germination (hypogeal in maize, epigeal in common bean) and hormones (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid) together account for differences in germination, emergence and growth; (b) distinguish growth from development and describe primary and secondary growth and apical dominance; (c) apply knowledge of hormones to plan rooting of stem cuttings in a tree nursery.
slo.skills: Constructing explanations (NGSS SEP 6) using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; developing and using models (SEP 2) by revising the Day 1 model; analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4) from germination tables and growth curves; engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7) during the Gallery Walk; planning investigations (SEP 3) for the nursery project; communicating scientific information in simple, clear English.
slo.attitudes: Unity: learners work harmoniously in groups to build and review the final explanation. Patriotism: learners value sharing seedlings with the school and community for environmental conservation. Learning to Learn: learners reflect on how their thinking changed since Day 1 and adjust accordingly. Citizenship: learners plan to solve community problems by sharing nursery seedlings. Financial Literacy: learners explore generating income by selling seedlings at a subsidised price. Prevention of Global Warming: learners recognise the role of tree planting in mitigating climate change. Appreciation of the importance of growth and development in plants.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 10 is the culminating lesson. Learners have gathered evidence on seed structure, dormancy, germination conditions, types of germination, primary and secondary growth, growth measurement and hormones. Now they bring everything together to answer the Driving Question about the farmer's maize and beans, compare their Day 1 and final models, and transfer their understanding to a real-life project, the tree nursery, which links to the KICD project and to community service.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only seeds, cuttings and materials that are untreated; seeds dressed with pesticide (often pink or purple coated) must not be handled or tasted. Wash hands after handling soil, onion juice, Aloe gel and cinnamon. Do not taste any materials. Use a clean, sharp knife or razor only under teacher supervision for cutting stems (teacher or one designated learner per group cuts at an angle; others observe). Keep Aloe sap away from eyes. Learners with allergies to onion, cinnamon or Aloe should observe and record rather than handle. Move carefully during the Gallery Walk to avoid collisions in crowded classrooms.

LESSONS.overview: This final lesson asks learners to answer the question: why did the farmer's maize and beans, planted on the same day after the same rain, germinate, emerge and grow differently? Learners begin by predicting how a farmer in Kakamega or Nyeri could improve germination and rooting of new plants. They then review the evidence collected across the unit (class germination tables, seed drawings, growth curves, hormone notes) in an evidence-sorting activity using Think-Pair-Share. In the Explain phase, they write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) final explanation and take part in a Gallery Walk with peer review. The class then closes the Driving Question Board (DQB), sorting questions into answered, partly answered and new questions. Finally, learners compare their Day 1 model with the final cumulative model and plan the tree nursery project using stem cuttings with bulb onion, Aloe and cinnamon as natural rooting hormone sources. The lesson requires only chart paper, previous learner notebooks, class data, simple drawings and locally available materials; no electricity or internet is required, and time-lapse video can be replaced with the teacher's printed photo sequence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the anchoring phenomenon: the farmer in Molo plants maize and beans on the same day after rain, but some seeds germinate quickly, some slowly, and some not at all even though they look healthy. Using the teacher's printed photo sequence (or the time-lapse video if available), they view the growth sequence once more. Individually they write a 3-minute prediction on a half sheet: 'If the farmer wanted to grow 200 mango and grevillea seedlings from stem cuttings for a school tree nursery in Machakos, what would help the cuttings form roots, and why?' Learners predict using what they know about auxins and plant growth. They then Think-Pair-Share with a partner and add one idea from the partner in a different colour.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Day 1 model charts and the DQB at the front. Say: 'Today is our final lesson. Today we will answer the farmer's puzzle and use our learning to start a tree nursery.' Show the photo sequence for 2 minutes. Ask: 'What puzzled us on Day 1?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to recall the puzzle. Pose the nursery prediction question and give 3 minutes of silent writing time. Say: 'Think first. Write your own idea before you talk.' Then give 2 minutes for pair talk. Circulate and listen for mention of hormones, auxins, cut surface, water, or light. Cold-call 4 pairs to share. Record predictions on the board under 'Our Nursery Predictions'. Do not correct yet; say: 'We will test these ideas against our evidence today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share: the prediction step surfaces learners' current ideas about hormones and rooting before they apply evidence, so that transfer of learning to a new context (stem cuttings) can be checked. Think-Pair-Share gives every learner thinking time and a low-risk chance to rehearse ideas, which supports participation in large classes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: tick learners who (1) write a prediction with a reason, (2) mention at least one hormone or growth factor such as auxins, water or oxygen, (3) add a partner's idea in a different colour. Oral probing: ask 'Why do you think that would help roots form?' Look for misconceptions such as 'cuttings need fertiliser to root' or 'hormones are only found in animals'. Record names of 5 learners whose predictions need follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 5 or 6, learners review the evidence collected across Lessons 1-9 using an Evidence Sorting Station. Each group receives a set of cards or uses their notebooks showing: (1) labelled drawings of maize (monocot) and bean (dicot) seeds, (2) class germination data for maize and beans under different conditions (water, no water, with and without air, cold vs warm), (3) results on dormancy-breaking (soaking, scarification), (4) hypogeal vs epigeal germination observations, (5) a seedling height growth curve, (6) notes on primary and secondary growth and (7) notes on auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and apical dominance. Groups sort evidence under three headings: 'Seed factors', 'Environmental factors' and 'Hormone and growth factors'. They then examine a set of prepared stem cuttings or photographs: hibiscus or sweet potato vine cuttings treated with crushed bulb onion, Aloe gel, cinnamon powder or water only (control), prepared by the teacher or earlier by the class, and record number of roots and days to rooting in a simple table.
framework.teacherMoves: Arrange evidence cards or ask learners to open notebooks to the marked pages. Say: 'You are scientists. Your job is to find which evidence explains the farmer's puzzle.' Give each group 10 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'Which piece of evidence shows why some seeds did not germinate?' and 'Where do you see the effect of water or oxygen in our data?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 2 members from different groups per question. When groups examine the cuttings, ask: 'What is different about the treated and untreated cuttings? What could be the cause?' If the real cuttings are unavailable, use the teacher-prepared table of results from the earlier class experiment. Remind learners to use simple scientific English, e.g. 'The bean seed absorbed water, so the seed coat softened.' Clarify difficult terms such as 'scarification', 'epigeal' and 'apical dominance' on the board. Move quickly between groups to ensure equipment and notebooks are shared fairly.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence sorting with Discussion and questioning: categorising prior evidence into seed, environment and hormone factors helps learners see that many causes act together rather than one cause alone, and prepares them to build a multi-part explanation. Observing the rooting results gives a new data set that tests whether their understanding of hormones transfers to a new context.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist indicators: (1) group places at least 6 of 8 evidence items under the correct heading, (2) learners point to specific data (e.g. 'Beans in dry cotton wool did not swell') when justifying, (3) learners read the rooting table accurately and identify the control. Oral probing: 'Why do we need a cutting with only water?' Listen for the idea of a control. Quick check: ask each group to name one piece of evidence for each of the three headings. Note groups that confuse dormancy with lack of water.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write a Final Explanation using the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) frame, individually after group discussion, to answer the Driving Question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' CLAIM: a clear statement naming the causes (e.g. seed structure and food stores, dormancy status, availability of water, oxygen and warmth, type of germination, hormone levels). EVIDENCE: at least three specific pieces of data from the unit (e.g. 'In our class test, 8 out of 10 soaked beans germinated compared with 3 out of 10 dry beans'; 'Maize remained underground with cotyledon (hypogeal) while bean cotyledons rose above ground (epigeal)'). REASONING: link evidence to biology ideas (e.g. 'Water activates enzymes and gibberellins that break down stored food, so the embryo can grow; the epigeal bean raises its seed leaves, so it emerges differently from maize'). Learners also explain differences in later growth: maize shows mostly primary growth and tall unbranched stem, while bean shows branching affected by apical dominance and auxins. After writing, groups pin their CER explanations and drawings on the wall for a Gallery Walk. Learners rotate every 3 minutes with sticky notes giving one 'star' (strength) and one 'step' (improvement) per display. They then return to their own work and revise it using the feedback.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the CER sentence frames on the board: 'We claim that ... Our evidence is ... This happens because ...'. Say: 'A good scientific explanation uses evidence from our own investigations, not just what we remember.' Give 12 minutes of writing time, with the first 2 minutes in silence. Circulate and ask: 'Which data from our class results supports that claim?' and 'Explain the link: why does that evidence make your claim true?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Before the Gallery Walk, model peer feedback with one example: 'Star: you used our germination numbers. Step: explain why water is needed.' Set the Gallery Walk for about 12 minutes, with groups rotating on a clap signal. Cold-call 4 learners afterwards to share one improvement they will make. Listen for misconceptions such as 'Maize has no dormancy' or 'hormones make seeds grow without water'. Address them: 'Check your evidence. Can a seed germinate without water in our test?' Allow learners to revise for 5 minutes. Use a whole-class check with a Kenyan example: 'A farmer in Kitale plants hybrid maize seeds that failed to germinate after planting in dry soil. What advice would you give?' Cold-call 3 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) builds understanding by requiring learners to connect data to scientific principles rather than list facts. The Gallery Walk with peer review engages learners in argument from evidence: they compare explanations, notice missing links and revise, which deepens understanding of multiple interacting causes. Revising after feedback supports Learning to Learn.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review rubric (3 levels) for CER: Claim names at least 3 causes; Evidence cites at least 3 specific class data or observations; Reasoning links each evidence item to a biological principle (water uptake, enzyme activation, hormone action, apical dominance). Observable indicators: learners use words such as 'because' and 'therefore', cite numbers from tables, and revise after feedback. Oral probing during revision: 'What did you change after the Gallery Walk?' Collect 5 CER explanations at random as a quick quiz-style check and note common gaps for later feedback.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board created in Lesson 1, which holds their questions (for example, 'Why did some healthy-looking seeds fail to germinate?', 'Why do bean cotyledons come above the ground but maize ones do not?', 'What makes stems grow taller and thicker?', 'How do hormones affect rooting?'). In groups, they take turns choosing a question card, deciding whether it is Answered, Partly answered or New, and placing it in the corresponding column on the board. For each answered question, a learner writes a one-sentence answer with the evidence and lesson number on a sticky note (e.g. 'Lesson 4: Beans in water at room temperature germinated; those with no water did not'). Learners also add new questions arising from the nursery project, such as 'Which natural hormone gives the most roots on mango cuttings?' or 'Can we sell seedlings at a profit if we use free onion and Aloe?'. They then complete a short exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB and say: 'Let us check how far our questions have been answered.' Invite 6 groups, each to handle 2-3 questions. Say: 'Choose a question. Tell us what evidence from which lesson answers it.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before calling on a group to defend its placement. Cold-call 5 learners to justify a card placement. If a question is partly answered, ask: 'What else do we need to find out?' Encourage learners to link to the farmer's puzzle: 'How does this answer help explain what happened in the farmer's field in Molo?' Give 3 minutes for adding new questions. Hand out exit tickets and give 4 minutes to write. Collect them at the door. Review a few tickets immediately to identify misconceptions to address next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the Driving Question Board: sorting questions by how well they have been answered makes learning visible and helps learners see how each lesson contributed to the main question. Adding new questions models how science generates further inquiry, and motivates the project phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners correctly place at least 80 percent of cards, cite the specific lesson and data to justify, and suggest at least one new relevant question. Exit ticket success criteria: names at least two pieces of evidence (e.g. germination counts, growth curve, rooting results) and links them to the driving question. Oral probing: 'Which question is still partly answered and why?' Note learners whose tickets list facts without linking them to the driving question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Day 1 model (a drawing and short explanation of why the farmer's maize and beans behaved differently) and place it next to a new, large final cumulative model drawn in their groups on chart paper. The final model shows: (1) labelled maize and bean seeds (seed coat, embryo, cotyledon(s), endosperm); (2) factors triggering germination (water, oxygen, warmth, dormancy breaking), with arrows to hormones (gibberellins, abscisic acid) in the seed; (3) hypogeal germination in maize and epigeal germination in bean with emergence heights; (4) primary growth at root and shoot tips, secondary growth in woody dicots, and apical dominance with auxins; (5) a growth curve (S-shaped) for seedling height. Using a different colour pen, learners mark on the Day 1 model what was missing or incorrect and write 'Then I thought... Now I know... because...' statements (at least 3). Finally, groups apply the model to the tree nursery project by drawing a plan for rooting stem cuttings of mango, grevillea or hibiscus: selecting healthy cuttings 15-20 cm, cutting just below a node, applying crushed bulb onion juice, Aloe gel or cinnamon powder (natural rooting hormone sources), planting in moist sandy soil in polythene tubes, shading, watering daily, and recording rooting. They list roles (Unity), a basic budget and a subsidised selling price (Financial Literacy), and where seedlings will be planted or shared in the community (Citizenship, Patriotism, Prevention of Global Warming).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Hold up your Day 1 model. What would you change now?' Allow 15 seconds of WAIT TIME. Cold-call 3 learners to name one change. Give groups 12 minutes to draw the final model and 5 minutes for the 'Then I thought... Now I know...' statements. Circulate and ask: 'Where does the hormone appear in your model, and what does it do?' and 'How does your model explain why maize cotyledon stays below ground?' Push for links: 'Where is the evidence for that arrow?' Then introduce the nursery plan: 'Our model says auxins stimulate root formation. How can we use onion, Aloe and cinnamon to help our cuttings root?' Give 8 minutes for planning, and remind learners about safety (no tasting, wash hands, teacher or one trained learner cuts stems). Cold-call 4 groups to present one key step and its scientific reason. Close by saying: 'You can now explain the farmer's puzzle and help your community plant trees.' Assign the nursery set-up as a follow-up task: groups bring cuttings, polythene tubes or tins and soil for the next practical session, and record weekly rooting data. Collect group models for a quick model check.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: comparing the Day 1 model with the final model makes conceptual change visible, so learners can see how evidence added mechanisms (hormones, dormancy, germination type, growth regions) to their initial ideas. Applying the model to the tree nursery is a transfer task that shows whether learners can use scientific explanations to solve a real community problem.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check indicators: final model includes at least 5 of the 6 required components (seed structures, germination conditions, hormones, hypogeal vs epigeal, primary/secondary growth and apical dominance, growth curve), labels are accurate, arrows show cause and effect, and at least 3 evidence-based 'Then I thought... Now I know...' statements are present. Nursery plan checklist: includes a control (water only), a hormone source with scientific reason, safe handling, and roles. Peer review: groups swap plans and give one star and one step. Record learners who still hold misconceptions (for example, 'hormones feed the cutting') and plan follow-up feedback.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) Did learners' final CER explanations include multiple interacting causes (seed structure, dormancy, water, oxygen, warmth, germination type, hormones) rather than a single cause? Which causes were most often missing? (2) How did learners' final models differ from their Day 1 models, and which learners showed the greatest conceptual change? (3) Which misconceptions persisted, such as confusing growth with development, thinking hormones are food, or thinking all seeds germinate in the same way? (4) Did the Gallery Walk and peer review help learners improve their explanations, and was the time sufficient in a large class? (5) How well did learners transfer their understanding of auxins to the tree nursery plan, and what support will they need to set up and monitor the nursery (materials, supervision, record keeping, and selling seedlings at a subsidised price)? (6) Did all learners, including those with limited access to textbooks, participate fully? Plan how to follow up weekly with the nursery data and revisit the DQB for remaining questions.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that maize and bean seeds differ in structure (monocot with endosperm vs dicot with cotyledons), that seeds failed to germinate without water, oxygen or warmth or when dormant, that maize germinates hypogeally and bean epigeally, that seedling height follows an S-shaped growth curve, and that stem cuttings treated with natural hormone sources such as bulb onion, Aloe or cinnamon rooted differently from the control.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that germination, emergence and growth depend on seed structure and food stores, dormancy and its breaking, water, oxygen and suitable temperature, type of germination, growth at meristems (primary and secondary growth), and plant hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid, including apical dominance. We also learned that growth is an increase in size while development involves changes in form and function.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The farmer's maize and beans differed because each seed had a different structure, dormancy status and germination type, and experienced different water, oxygen and warmth conditions around the seed. These factors changed the levels and action of hormones such as gibberellins and abscisic acid in the seed and auxins in the growing plant, which control when the embryo grows, how the seedling emerges, and how the stem and roots grow. We can apply this to grow tree seedlings from cuttings by using natural rooting hormone sources, and share the seedlings to benefit our community and help reduce global warming.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Biology Grade 11: Growth and Development in Plants (Sub-strand 2.2)
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: You are a scientist helping a farmer in Nakuru County. The farmer planted maize and beans on the same day after the long rains. Some seeds germinated within a few days, some took longer, and some healthy-looking seeds never sprouted. As the plants grew, they also differed in height, thickness, root depth and branching. Your task is to write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) explanation that answers the driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants? Use evidence from our unit: your seed drawings and dissections, the dormancy and germination investigations, the stem sections, the growth curves and the hormone notes. Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use labelled drawings and arrows where they help. In Section 4 you will also revise your Day 1 model. Write in full sentences and use the scientific words we have learned.

sections.title: Section 1: Seed structure and food supply
sections.prompt: Compare a maize grain and a bean seed. (a) Name the main structures you saw in each, and say what each one does. (b) Describe how these two seeds differ in the number of cotyledons and in where the food is stored. (c) Explain how these differences could affect the way each seedling emerges and grows early on. Refer to your dissections of soaked seeds.
sections.exemplar: (a) Maize grain: one cotyledon (the scutellum), a large endosperm that stores food, a protective coleoptile around the shoot and a coleorhiza around the root. Bean seed: a testa (seed coat) that protects the seed, a hilum (scar where it was attached), a micropyle (small pore for water entry), two large cotyledons that store food, a plumule (the future shoot) and a radicle (the future root). (b) Maize is a monocot with one cotyledon and its food is stored mainly in the endosperm. Bean is a dicot with two cotyledons, and its food is stored in the cotyledons. (c) The embryo uses the stored food for energy and building materials until the leaves can make food. Because the stores are held in different places, the two seedlings emerge differently: the maize shoot is protected by the coleoptile as it pushes up, while the bean seedling carries its food-storing cotyledons with it. So seed structure is one reason maize and beans did not behave the same way, even when planted on the same day after the same rain.

sections.title: Section 2: Dormancy and germination conditions
sections.prompt: Some of the farmer's seeds looked healthy but did not germinate, and others were late. Write a CER explanation using the two investigations we did. Claim: give two different reasons why seeds planted after the same rain may germinate late or fail. Evidence: describe what you observed in the dormancy treatments (control, sandpaper, warm water, leaching or chilling) and in the germination sets (water, air and warmth; dry; little oxygen; cool; boiled seeds). Reasoning: explain why each result happened, using the words dormancy, viable, water, oxygen and temperature.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Seeds can germinate late or fail because they are dormant, or because one of the conditions needed for germination is missing or the seed is not alive. Evidence: In the dormancy investigation, seeds that were rubbed with sandpaper, soaked in warm water or leached took up water and responded sooner than the untreated control seeds. In the germination sets, seeds with water, air and warmth germinated. Dry seeds did not germinate, seeds submerged with little oxygen did not germinate normally, cool seeds were slower, and boiled (non-viable) seeds did not germinate at all. Reasoning: A dormant seed is alive but rests even when conditions look suitable, for example because of a hard seed coat that blocks water, chemical inhibitors, or an embryo that is not ready. Scarifying, warm-water soaking and leaching break this block, which is why treated seeds responded sooner. Germination needs water to start the seed's chemical reactions, oxygen for respiration to release energy, and a suitable temperature. Boiled seeds are dead (not viable), so they cannot germinate whatever the conditions. In the farmer's field, waterlogged soil, dry patches, cool spots, dormant seeds or dead seeds could therefore each explain why some seeds were late or never sprouted.

sections.title: Section 3: How the seedlings emerge and keep growing
sections.prompt: (a) Compare how maize and bean seedlings emerge from the soil. Use the terms hypogeal and epigeal. (b) Explain how primary growth and secondary growth differ, and where in the plant each one happens. (c) Use your stem-section observations to explain why a bean plant can become thicker and branch while maize grows mainly in length. (d) Describe the shape of the growth curve you plotted and what it tells you about growth over time.
sections.exemplar: (a) Maize shows hypogeal germination: the cotyledon stays below the ground and the shoot grows up. Bean shows epigeal germination: the cotyledons are lifted above the ground as the stem grows. (b) Primary growth is an increase in length. It happens at the apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots, where cells divide and then elongate. Secondary growth is an increase in girth (thickness). It happens at lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, in dicots and woody plants such as Grevillea and Eucalyptus. (c) In the bean (dicot) stem, the vascular bundles were in a ring with cambium between the xylem and phloem, so the stem can thicken. In the maize (monocot) stem, the bundles were scattered and there was no cambium, so maize grows mainly in length. (d) The growth curve was S-shaped: a slow start (lag phase), a rapid growth phase, then a levelling off. This shows that the rate of growth changes over time and that the two crops can differ in how fast and how tall they grow even when planted on the same day. Maize grew faster and taller than beans in the same period.

sections.title: Section 4: Hormones and your final CER explanation
sections.prompt: Write your final explanation to answer the driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants? Claim: state your answer in one or two sentences. Evidence: give at least three pieces of evidence from different lessons, including at least one about hormones (for example, the bean seedling with its tip removed). Reasoning: link your evidence to your claim and explain how hormones work together with water, oxygen, temperature and seed structure. Finally, say how your Day 1 model or drawing has changed, and describe one thing you added.
sections.exemplar: Claim: The farmer's maize and beans differed because their seeds have different structures, because the seeds met different conditions (water, oxygen, warmth) and had different dormancy status, and because growth in the plants is driven by different meristems and controlled by hormones. Evidence: (1) Maize has one cotyledon and a large endosperm, while bean has two cotyledons, and they emerge differently (maize hypogeal, bean epigeal). (2) Seeds with water, air and warmth germinated, while dry, low-oxygen, cool or boiled seeds did not, and seeds with dormancy-breaking treatments responded sooner than the control. (3) The bean stem has cambium and can thicken and branch, while the maize stem has none and grows mainly in length, and both showed S-shaped growth curves. (4) A bean seedling with its tip removed grew more side branches but was shorter, while the intact seedling grew taller with few branches. Reasoning: Stored food and seed structure decide how the embryo is supplied and how the seedling emerges. Water, oxygen and suitable temperature allow the embryo to grow, and dormancy or dead seeds explain why some healthy-looking seeds did not sprout. Once growing, cell division and elongation at apical meristems give length, and cambium gives thickness. Hormones coordinate all this: gibberellins and abscisic acid affect dormancy and germination time, auxin from the shoot tip causes apical dominance and shoot elongation, and cytokinins affect branching. Removing the tip removed the auxin, which released the side buds, so this supports the role of hormones. Growth is an increase in size, while development is the change in form and function as the seed becomes a mature plant. My Day 1 model only showed a seed and a shoot. I revised it to add the labelled seed structures, the conditions water, oxygen and warmth, dormancy, the meristems, and arrows for hormones.

sections.title: Section 5: Applying your understanding
sections.prompt: A farmer in Kakamega or Nyeri wants to improve germination and rooting for a school tree nursery. Give two practical pieces of advice, and explain each one using ideas from this unit. Mention one natural rooting source you tested.
sections.exemplar: Advice 1: Check that the seeds are viable and plant them in moist but not waterlogged soil in a warm place. Seeds need water, oxygen and suitable warmth to germinate, and waterlogged soil removes oxygen. If seeds have a hard coat and seem dormant, scarify them with sandpaper or soak them in warm water to let water in, because dormancy can be broken this way. Advice 2: To help stem cuttings root, treat them with a natural rooting source such as bulb onion, Aloe or cinnamon. In our nursery test, cuttings treated this way rooted differently from the control. Auxins are plant hormones that encourage rooting, so these sources can help the cuttings form roots. Healthy tree seedlings can then be shared to benefit the community and help reduce global warming.

SUMMARY_TABLE.subStrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?

lessons.title: The Farmer's Puzzle: Why Do Maize and Beans Behave Differently After the Same Rain?
lessons.observed: In the time-lapse videos and pictures of maize and beans planted together after rain, we observed that the seeds germinated at different times, the root and shoot emerged, stems became taller and thicker, roots went deeper, some plants developed branches, and some seeds did not germinate even though they looked healthy.
lessons.learned: We learned that the same rain and same planting day do not give the same result for every seed, and that we do not yet know what causes these differences. We drew our first models and learned that ideas can change when we find evidence. We also learned that we need to understand what growth and development mean.
lessons.explained: Our first explanation (not yet marked): maize and bean plants may grow differently because of differences in their seeds and in what each seed needs, such as water, air and warmth. We do not yet have evidence, so we have posted our questions on the Driving Question Board. Our next question is: What is growth and development?

lessons.title: Meaning of Growth and Development; Structure of Monocot and Dicot Seeds
lessons.observed: We observed and dissected soaked maize grains and bean seeds, and saw that maize has one cotyledon (scutellum) with a large endosperm and protective coleoptile and coleorhiza, while beans have two large cotyledons, a testa, hilum, micropyle, plumule and radicle.
lessons.learned: Growth is a permanent increase in size, dry mass or cell number, while development is the change in form and function as cells differentiate. Seed structures have specific functions such as protection, food storage, absorbing water and forming the new root and shoot.
lessons.explained: Maize and beans are built differently, so they store and supply food to the embryo in different ways, which may partly explain differences in emergence and early growth. Since some healthy-looking seeds still failed to germinate, other factors, such as seed dormancy, must also be investigated.

lessons.title: Seed Dormancy: Why Do Some Healthy-Looking Seeds Refuse to Germinate?
lessons.observed: We examined maize, bean and other local seeds with hand lenses, noting hard and thin seed coats and how much water the seeds absorbed. We set up control, scarified, warm-water-soaked and leached/chilled seeds and recorded changes over time.
lessons.learned: Seed dormancy is a resting state in which a living seed fails to germinate even when conditions seem suitable. Causes include a hard impermeable seed coat, chemical inhibitors, an immature embryo, and unsuitable environmental cues. Dormancy can be broken by scarification, soaking in warm water, leaching, chilling (stratification) and after-ripening. Dormancy helps seeds survive unfavourable seasons and spreads germination over time.
lessons.explained: Some seeds in the farmer's field do not germinate or are delayed even after the same rain because they are dormant: their hard seed coats may block water entry, inhibitors may need to be washed away or broken down, or their embryos may not be ready. Evidence: in our containers, treated seeds took up water and responded sooner than untreated controls. This explains part of the difference in germination between maize and beans, but we still need to find out how germination occurs once dormancy is broken.

lessons.title: Germination: Process, Types and Conditions Necessary for Germination in Maize and Bean Seeds
lessons.observed: We set up maize and bean seeds in containers with different conditions (moist and open to air, dry, submerged with little oxygen, cool, and boiled seeds) and compared them over several days. We also examined and drew germinating maize and bean seedlings. Record the number of seeds germinated in each container and the differences between how the maize and bean seedlings emerged.
lessons.learned: Seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate, and they must be alive (viable) and not dormant. Germination starts with water uptake, then the radicle emerges, then the plumule. Maize shows hypogeal germination (cotyledon stays below ground), while bean shows epigeal germination (cotyledons are lifted above ground).
lessons.explained: Seeds planted on the same day after the same rain can germinate at different times, or fail, because of differences in moisture, oxygen (for example in waterlogged soil), temperature, seed viability and dormancy. Maize and beans also emerge differently because of their type of germination. After emergence, how do plants show growth? This will be investigated in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Growth: How Do Plants Show Growth?
lessons.observed: We observed prepared slides, photomicrographs or hand-cut sections of young bean (dicot) and maize (monocot) stems and a cut log from a woody tree with annual rings. We saw vascular bundles in a ring in the bean stem with cambium between xylem and phloem, scattered bundles in maize with no cambium, and secondary xylem, bark and rings in the older woody stem.
lessons.learned: We learned that primary growth is an increase in length produced by apical meristems at shoot and root tips, while secondary growth is an increase in girth produced by the vascular cambium and cork cambium in dicots and woody plants. Maize (a monocot) mainly shows primary growth, whereas bean and trees such as Grevillea and Eucalyptus show both. This raises the question: How can you measure growth in plants?
lessons.explained: Using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning, we explained that part of the difference in how maize and bean plants grow after germination is due to stem structure: the bean stem has cambium that allows thickening and branching, while the maize stem lacks cambium and grows mainly in length. This adds to our model that differences in germination and growth depend on seed structure, germination conditions, and the meristems that drive growth.

lessons.title: Where Does a Maize or Bean Plant Grow? Measuring Growth and Regions of Growth in Seedlings
lessons.observed: We marked maize and bean seedlings at equal intervals and measured how the marks moved apart over time. We also measured seedling height at intervals and plotted a growth curve. The marks near the root tip and shoot tip moved apart the most, and the curve showed a slow start, a rapid middle phase, and a levelling-off phase.
lessons.learned: Growth in length is concentrated in specific regions (apical meristems at the root and shoot tips, followed by elongation), while stems thicken through secondary growth in some plants such as beans. Growth can be measured and shown on a growth curve that is S-shaped. Maize and bean seedlings grow at different rates and in different ways.
lessons.explained: The maize and bean plants planted on the same day differ in height, root depth and branching because growth occurs in particular regions and at different rates in each plant type and over time. The sigmoid growth curve and the types of growth (primary and secondary) help explain these differences. What controls the cells at the tips to divide and elongate is still unknown, which raises the next question: Do we have hormones in plants?

lessons.title: Plant Hormones: What Controls Growth in Maize and Bean Seedlings?
lessons.observed: We watched a video and read about the major plant hormones (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene) and recorded where each is made and what it does in the plant.
lessons.learned: Hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate germination, dormancy, shoot and root growth, branching and fruit ripening. They work together with environmental factors such as water, oxygen and temperature.
lessons.explained: Differences in germination, emergence and growth between maize and bean plants can partly be explained by hormone balance: for example, gibberellins and abscisic acid affect dormancy and germination time, auxin affects shoot elongation and apical dominance, and cytokinins affect branching. To compare growth we now need to measure it.

lessons.title: Measuring Growth: Seedling Height, Stem Width and Growth Curves of Maize and Beans
lessons.observed: We measured the height and stem width of maize and bean seedlings over time and plotted growth curves. Both curves were S-shaped, with a slow start, a rapid growth phase and a levelling-off phase, but maize grew faster and taller than beans in the same period.
lessons.learned: Growth can be measured as height, stem width, mass or leaf area. A growth curve shows that growth rate changes over time (lag, exponential and stationary phases). Maize and beans differ in growth rate and pattern even when planted on the same day.
lessons.explained: The growth rate changes because of food stores, cell division and elongation, leaf area for photosynthesis and the type of plant. Something inside the plant may be controlling the timing and speed of growth, so we ask: Do we have hormones in plants?

lessons.title: Role of Hormones in Plant Growth and Development: Why Do Maize and Bean Plants Grow Differently?
lessons.observed: We observed that a bean seedling with its tip removed grew more side branches but was shorter, while the intact seedling grew taller with few branches. We also saw (in the video or chart) how plant parts respond to hormones, e.g. bending toward light and rooting of cuttings, and we read that gibberellins, abscisic acid, cytokinins, auxins and ethylene each control different parts of growth.
lessons.learned: We learned that hormones are chemical messengers that control germination, dormancy, cell elongation, branching, rooting and fruit ripening. Auxin from the shoot tip causes apical dominance, and removing the tip releases side buds. Farmers use this knowledge when pruning tea in Kericho, rooting cuttings in tree nurseries and ripening bananas and mangoes.
lessons.explained: Hormones help explain why maize and beans planted together on the same day can germinate, emerge and grow differently: the balance of gibberellins and abscisic acid affects whether a seed breaks dormancy, and auxin and cytokinins control shoot growth and branching, with differences in species and seed condition changing the outcome. These internal signals work together with water, oxygen, temperature and seed structure to produce the differences we saw in the farmer's field.

lessons.title: Synthesis and Application: Explaining the Farmer's Maize and Beans and Planning the Tree Nursery
lessons.observed: We observed that maize and bean seeds differ in structure (monocot with endosperm vs dicot with cotyledons), that seeds failed to germinate without water, oxygen or warmth or when dormant, that maize germinates hypogeally and bean epigeally, that seedling height follows an S-shaped growth curve, and that stem cuttings treated with natural hormone sources such as bulb onion, Aloe or cinnamon rooted differently from the control.
lessons.learned: We learned that germination, emergence and growth depend on seed structure and food stores, dormancy and its breaking, water, oxygen and suitable temperature, type of germination, growth at meristems (primary and secondary growth), and plant hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid, including apical dominance. We also learned that growth is an increase in size while development involves changes in form and function.
lessons.explained: The farmer's maize and beans differed because each seed had a different structure, dormancy status and germination type, and experienced different water, oxygen and warmth conditions around the seed. These factors changed the levels and action of hormones such as gibberellins and abscisic acid in the seed and auxins in the growing plant, which control when the embryo grows, how the seedling emerges, and how the stem and roots grow. We can apply this to grow tree seedlings from cuttings by using natural rooting hormone sources, and share the seedlings to benefit our community and help reduce global warming.
